chapters.summary: Staff welcomes attendees to the Committee on Education hearing, asks to silence electronics and not approach the dais, and directs testifiers to fill out slips with the Sergeant at Arms.
chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and instructs witnesses to sign in

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to the New York City Council hearing on the Committee on Education.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please silence all electronics and do not approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you are testifying today, make sure you have filled out a slip with the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Any other questions or concerns, please reach a Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz introduces himself as a public school alum and former teacher, notes outreach from parents about bus service, especially families of children with disabilities who sacrifice jobs and income.
chapters.title: Chair Dinowitz opens hearing with personal background on school bus struggles

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I'm Councilmember Eric Dinowitz, proud New York City Public School alum, former New York City Public School teacher and chair of the Committee on Education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Welcome to today's oversight hearing examining school bus transportation services in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I can't begin to express how much outreach I've gotten, not just about this hearing, but since taking office, since even when I was a teacher, how many parents struggled with the school bus service here in our city.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it was always kids with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I think the heartbreaking thing is, you know, when I started teaching at 21, I wasn't a parent.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I didn't know really how much parents sacrifice for their kids, but particularly how much parents of kids with disabilities sacrifice for their kids.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How many parents of kids with disabilities have to quit their job to become full-time advocates for their children?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Or whose spouse has to take a second job to pay for services that they shouldn't have to pay for?

chapters.summary: He describes emails and calls about children missing buses, waiting an hour, soiling themselves on two-hour trips, and the unconscionable conditions.
chapters.title: Dinowitz recounts missed buses and long rides for students

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And with all that, as they fight for...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: for their children, for their services, for just what every other kid gets, like a good education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Once they get that, they then have to continue that fight just to get their kid to school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It is heartbreaking and unconscionable to receive emails and phone calls.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That a child didn't get on the bus because it never came, that they were waiting for an hour for the bus, that they soiled themselves on the bus because the trip was two hours long.

chapters.summary: School buses are critical for students with disabilities, foster care, and temporary housing; he describes waiting in freezing temperatures and missing instruction and work.
chapters.title: Dinowitz highlights impact on students with disabilities and foster care

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: School bus service plays a vital role in ensuring access to education for all of our students in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: School buses are particularly critical for some of our city's most vulnerable kids, kids with disabilities, students in foster care, and students in temporary housing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They rely on school buses to get to and from school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And again, year after year, we hear these disturbing accounts of conditions these students endure, if they endure them at all, just to get the public education they deserve and to which they are entitled.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And imagine being that kid with a disability, waiting outside in freezing temperature for that school bus that never arrives.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the parent, your parent, has no way of knowing whether the bus is simply running late or isn't coming at all.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And by the time you find another way to go to school, you've missed the hours of instruction.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And critical services you depend on, your parents may have missed hours of

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: work or spent money that they don't have to get you to school, to get you that education that you deserve.

chapters.summary: He asks listeners to imagine riding a bus with broken AC and parents not knowing where their child is, especially for nonverbal students.
chapters.title: Dinowitz describes overheated buses and missing child fears

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And think about the hottest school day you've ever experienced.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And imagine riding to school on a bus with broken air conditioning, arriving overheated, dehydrated, and drenched in sweat.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Would you be able to focus on learning after experiencing those conditions?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And imagine being that parent waiting for your child to come home from school, only to find that the bus isn't coming and you have no way to reach anyone who can tell you where your child is.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The fear of having no idea where your child is, is unthinkable.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Again, particularly for parents of kids with disabilities who already face other challenges, particularly for parents of kids who are nonverbal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But families who rely on school bus transportation across New York City report experiences like these too often.

chapters.summary: He cites a 2025 Comptroller audit finding DOE lacks effective systems, notes VIA missed deadlines and concerns about infrastructure, and asks what concrete steps DOE is taking.
chapters.title: Dinowitz blames DOE for systemic failures and VIA delays

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Ultimately, responsibility for addressing these systemic failures lies with the Department of Education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A 2025 audit by the New York City Comptroller found that the DOE lacks effective systems to investigate the causes of service failures or its contracted bus companies accountable.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In recent years, we've been told that VIA would address longstanding inefficiencies in the school bus system.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yet, implementation deadlines have been missed, and many have raised

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: concerns about whether VIA has the infrastructure or expertise necessary to fulfill its contractual obligations.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I would add that while we have the controller's reports, we have passed numerous pieces of legislation here in this council, data transparency, to empower parents to hold the DOE accountable.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And unfortunately, year after year, including this year, those reports are transmitted late to the New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So today we will ask the DOE's Office of People Transportation, what concrete steps are you taking to improve school bus service for our children?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How are you making the system more efficient and safer for our students?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And how are you holding contractors accountable for delivering the services they are contractually obligated to provide?

chapters.summary: He thanks Speaker Menin for joining and for leadership on these issues.
chapters.title: Dinowitz thanks Speaker Menin and yields for opening remarks

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn it over to Speaker Menon for her opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'd like to thank you for joining us today's hearing and thank you for your leadership and partnership on these important issues.

chapters.summary: Menin thanks Chair Dinowitz and colleagues, notes DOE's $39 billion budget is 30% of city budget, and emphasizes Council's oversight and transparency role.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin thanks committee and frames DOE budget oversight

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Dinnowitz.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you for holding this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I also want to thank all of my colleagues who are here and particularly thank Council Members Ressler and Juan for the legislation that will be heard today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So the Department of Education is, as we all know, the largest city agency in terms of its budget, amounting to $39 billion

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: this year as of the November plan, which is about 30% of our overall city budget.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It goes without saying that the city council...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Council takes its oversight role very seriously and we are committed to transparency about how a third of our taxpayer dollars are being spent.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: DOE spends billions of dollars a year on outside contracts alone.

chapters.summary: She notes pupil transportation is DOE's third largest contract category at $2.28 billion in FY2027, up from $1.46 billion in FY2021, yet service has not improved.
chapters.title: Menin details growth in pupil transportation spending

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In March and April of this year, we asked DOE to review, for us really to get that review that we needed of about 579 of those contracts.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Pupil transportation is DOE's third largest contract category at $2.28 billion in fiscal 2027.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: DOE spent $2.1 billion on pupil transportation in fiscal year 2026, which is up $634 million

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: from the $1.46 billion spent just five years earlier in fiscal year 2021.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yet this growth has quite frankly not led to improved service.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: More taxpayer dollars are being spent than ever before, and yet New Yorkers are not experiencing any benefit.

chapters.summary: She mentions the 2013 strike, 52 companies signing an emergency extension, contracts dating to the 1970s, and VIA's missed 2020 and 2021 deadlines despite a $51.7 million contract.
chapters.title: Menin recounts decades of bus contract disputes and VIA failures

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: School bus contracts have been tied up in disputes for decades, mayor after mayor.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In 2013, as we all know, drivers went on strike for more than a month over job protections and new contracts.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And just last fall, with their contracts already expired, all 52 bus companies signed a 30-day emergency extension to keep the buses running.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: before eventually signing a three-year renewal of their contracts, many of which date back all the way to the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So what are New Yorkers getting for their money?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In 2019, DOE hired Via Transportation to track buses, track students, and build better routes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Student tracking data was due in August 2020.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: New routing was due in December 2021.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: DOE renewed that contract in 2024, bringing its total contract value to $51.7 million.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yet, despite the city having paid VIA over $35 million since 2019, as of last December, as you heard, the controller found that the new routing technology still had not been implemented.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: DOE says it is only now phasing out its old routing software.

chapters.summary: She says DOE could have assessed $44.3 million in penalties but only assessed $1.7 million, and could not prove collection; students with disabilities pay the price.
chapters.title: Menin criticizes DOE for leaving $44 million in penalties unassessed

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: DOE has also left money on the table.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Let's be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In the 2024 to 2025 school year, DOE could have assessed $44.3 million in penalties against bus companies whose drivers did not log in to the tracking app.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: However, it only assessed $1.7 million.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The year before, as complaints about busing rose sharply, DOE did not hold corrective action meetings or a required corrective action plan from any bus company.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And DOE could not show the controller's auditors proof that it

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: actually collected the penalties that it says that it assess.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Our students are paying the price, especially our students with disabilities, who are our most vulnerable students, the students that need our help the most, and their families, of course.

chapters.summary: Nearly seven weeks into the school year, advocates still working with kindergarten families without bus service; current contracts expire June 30, 2028, and a rebid takes 18 months.
chapters.title: Menin highlights kindergarteners without bus service and ticking contract clock

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Nearly seven weeks into this school year,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Advocates were still working with families of kindergarten students who had not yet attended school because a bus service was not in place.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This is shocking.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's unconscionable.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Time is running out.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The current bus contracts expire on June 30th, 2028.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: DOE has estimated that a full

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Rebid would take about 18 months, which means the clock is ticking before they actually expire again.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Last December, DOE told the controller it was focused on opening up a new procurement for school buses.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So today, we want to know, where does that new...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Solicitation stand?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is DOE now collecting the penalties its contracts already allow?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And how will DOE make sure the next contracts deliver the services that New Yorkers are paying for?

chapters.summary: She thanks the chair and returns the floor.
chapters.title: Menin yields back to Chair Dinowitz

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I'll now turn it back over to Chair Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: He thanks Speaker Menin for highlighting both moral and fiscal issues, including paying for contracts and not assessing fines.
chapters.title: Dinowitz thanks Menin and notes fiscal and moral imperative

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Minna.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Again, thank you for your partnership and leadership and highlighting not just the moral imperative,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: but the fiscal one as well, that we are paying for contracts,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and not assessing fines are just two of the critical elements I appreciate you highlighting in your remarks.

chapters.summary: Intro 835, sponsored by Councilmember Restler, would require DOE to report monthly on early and late pickups and drop-offs, missed pickups, and maintain an online public dashboard.
chapters.title: Dinowitz introduces Intro 835 school bus performance dashboard

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're also hearing two pieces of legislation today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Introduction 835, sponsored by Councilmember Lincoln Ressler, would require the DOE to report information related to school bus on-time performance.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: DOE would be required to report monthly on early and late school bus pickups and drop-offs from home and from school, the amount of time and minutes that bus routes were early or late, and missed pickups and drop-offs, among other data points.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: An officer agency chosen by the mayor would be required to maintain an online dashboard

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: that presents the reported data to the public in an accessible and easy to understand manner.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Having access to this type of data on a public dashboard would allow the public to gain a better understanding of the performance of our city's school buses and hold both the DOE and underperforming vendors and contracts accountable.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I am proud to be a co-prime sponsor of this legislation with Councilmember Ressler, and I'd now like to turn it over to him for some remarks on his legislation.

chapters.summary: Restler thanks Dinowitz and Menin, notes 150,000 students ride school buses daily, more than New Haven's population, with over 40% having disabilities and 6,000 in temporary housing or foster care.
chapters.title: Restler thanks colleagues and describes 150,000 daily bus riders

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I am grateful for your leadership on this topic and for your holding this hearing today and really want to thank you for your partnership on this.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really want to thank Speaker Menon, who is deeply committed to making government work better.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And this is an area that has been long overdue for reform.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, while thankfully the vast majority of students take

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: public transit, or walk to school, we have 150,000 students every single day who are on school buses.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just to give a sense of scale, that's more than the entire population of New Haven.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For those students, over 40% of whom have disabilities, about 70,000 students, and over 6,000 students are in temporary housing or foster care, school buses are their vital connection between home and school.

chapters.summary: He reports almost 90,000 delayed routes last year, 15,000 parent calls, 56,000 children late over an hour, and says there is no comprehensive data on worst vendors; Intro 835 would create a public database.
chapters.title: Restler cites 90,000 delayed routes and calls for data

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But last year, there were almost 90,000 delayed routes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There were 15,000 calls from parents about late pickups and arrivals.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just to give a sense of scale, 90,000 late routes means that there are 500 late routes every single school day.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Last year, there were 56,000 children who were late over an hour to get to school, missing precious time in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But the truth is, we don't fully understand the scale and nature of this problem.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There is no comprehensive data on how often school buses are late and which vendors are the worst performing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we're not using data, therefore, to improve routes and fix issues.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In the year 2026, there's just no reason why we shouldn't be harnessing technology to track every bus at all times to optimize routes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's frankly embarrassing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Intro 835 would require a publicly accessible online database so that we can track metrics on every single bus, every single day, and finally hold these school bus companies accountable.

chapters.summary: He appreciates DOE's VIA app and scorecards, but says NYC has renewed the same contracts since 1979 and needs new contracts with companies committed to modernization, citing Nice Bus as an example.
chapters.title: Restler praises DOE tracking but calls for new bus contracts

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really do appreciate that the DOE, led by Deputy Chancellor Moran, has taken important steps to improve bus transparency and tracking through the VIA app and other measures, including their new scorecards.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I look forward to hearing more about how that has been working.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Ultimately, we need new bus school contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: NYC has been renewing the same school bus contracts since 1979, which for the record is before I was born.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We need new school bus, I know you can't tell, but it's true.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know, I know, sad, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Not before me.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Gail, I'm not making any comments about that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We need new school bus contracts with companies that are absolutely committed to modernization and change.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We have a great example with Nice Bus, which is based in the 33rd Council District, a nonprofit that has been innovating with technology to track buses, improve safety, and even transition us to electric school buses.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's what we should be expecting from every single school bus company that wants to do business with New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The transparency legislation, the dashboard that we're creating in Intro 835 will help us get rid of the school bus companies that have been, frankly, failing our students for too many decades.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is how we generate the change that we deserve.

chapters.summary: He thanks Chair Dinowitz and Speaker Menin.
chapters.title: Restler concludes remarks on Intro 835

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Denowitz and Speaker Menon.

chapters.summary: Resolution 735, sponsored by Councilmember Julie Won and Dinowitz, calls on the state to pass S.1018/A.8440 to protect school bus workers' wages and benefits during employer transitions and prioritize experienced drivers.
chapters.title: Dinowitz introduces Resolution 735 on state school bus contracts

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We'll also be considering Resolution No.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: 735, sponsored by Councilmember Julie One and myself, calling on the New York State Legislature to pass and the Governor to sign.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Senate Bill 1018 and Assembly Bill 8440 to amend the education law in relation to contracts for the transportation of school children.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: These bills would amend the state education law to, quote, protect school bus workers'wage and benefits during transitions between employers in New York City, as well as prioritize the hiring of experienced school bus drivers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: To ensure high safety standards for students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The state bill would ensure that experienced school bus drivers, mechanics, dispatchers, and attendants retain their jobs, wages, and benefits when contracts change hands,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and that the city continues to benefit from their experience and expertise and end a longstanding quagmire in the city related to rebidding school bus contracts.

chapters.summary: He acknowledges colleagues present and on Zoom, and thanks Chief of Staff Jenna Klaus, Legislative Director Theo Solter, and Education Committee staff including Alejandro Carvajal, Chloe Rivera, Katie Salina, Andrew Lane Lawless, and Grace Amato.
chapters.title: Dinowitz recognizes attending Council members and committee staff

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'd also like to recognize my colleagues who are present today, including council members Brewer, Wong, Lewis, Ressler, Narcisse, Shulman, De La Rosa, Gutierrez, Joseph, Lee,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and on Zoom we have Farias.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I would like to remind, I'd also like to recognize and thank

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: my Chief of Staff, Jenna Klaus, my Legislative and Budget Director, Theo Solter, and the Education Committee staff, including Senior Legislative Counsel, Alejandro Carvajal, Senior Legislative Policy Analyst, Chloe Rivera, Legislative Policy Analyst, Katie Salina,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Principal Financial Analyst Andrew Lane Lawless, Senior Financial Analyst Grace Amato, along with other members of the Council's Finance Division, Oversight and Investigation Division, and the data team for their work on today's hearing, even

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: minutes leading up to this hearing.

chapters.summary: He reminds witnesses to fill out slips, notes no votes today, limits testimony to two minutes per person and member questions to five minutes, and asks witnesses to state their name for the record.
chapters.title: Dinowitz outlines witness slip and testimony rules

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I would like to remind everyone who wishes to testify in person today that you must fill out a witness slip, which you can find on the desk of the sergeant at arms near the entrance of this room.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Please fill out the slip even if you have already registered in advance that you will be testifying in person today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I also want to point out that we will not be voting on any legislation today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: To allow as many people as possible to testify, testimony will be limited to two minutes per person, whether you are testifying in person or on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I am also going to ask my colleagues to limit their questions and comments to five minutes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Please note that generally, witnesses who are here in person will testify before those who are signed on to the Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We've also been joined by Councilmember Susan Zhuang.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: As a reminder to all of our witnesses, please state your name prior to your testimony for the record.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If anyone here requires an accessible version of a presentation given at today's hearing, please email testimony at council.nyc.gov.

chapters.summary: He calls on each witness individually, asks them to raise their right hands and affirm to tell the truth and respond honestly.
chapters.title: Dinowitz administers affirmation to mayoral administration witnesses

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Now, in accordance with the rules of the Council, I will administer the affirmation to the witnesses from the mayoral administration.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I will call on each of you individually for a response.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Please raise your right hands.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: He names Kevin Moran, John Hammer, John Benson, and Fumita Salim, and tells them to begin and state their names for the record.
chapters.title: Dinowitz introduces first DOE panel

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we have on our first panel from the public schools, Kevin Moran, John Hammer, John Benson,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and Fumita Salim.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You may begin your testimony when ready, and please state your name for the record.

chapters.summary: Moran states he is Deputy Chancellor for School Operations and introduces John Benson, John Hammer, Lanika Parker-Moore, Fumita Salim, and April Leong.
chapters.title: Deputy Chancellor Moran introduces DOE panel

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Kevin Moran, Deputy Chancellor for Operations.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Speaker Menon, Chair Dendowitz, members of the Committee on Education, and members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: My name is Kevin Moran, and I serve as the Deputy Chancellor for School Operations for the New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I am joined by my colleagues, John Benson, Deputy Senior Executive Director of the Office of People Transportation,

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: John Hammer, Chief of the Division of Inclusive and Accessible Learning.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Lanika Parker-Moore, Executive Director of Ridership and Support from OPT.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Fامita Salim, the Executive Director of Access and Eligibility at OPT.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And April Leong, Chief of Students in Temporary Housing and Foster Care.

chapters.summary: He thanks the Council, underscores Chancellor Samuels' focus on safe reliable transportation, acknowledges bus drivers and matrons who start as early as 3-4 a.m., and says access to learning starts with getting to school safely.
chapters.title: Moran testifies on importance of reliable school bus service

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I appreciate the opportunity to appear before you today to discuss transportation services in New York City and Intro 835.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We value our partnership with the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: and appreciate your commitment to supporting the needs of students and families across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: First, I want to clearly underscore the importance of school bus service to this administration.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Chancellor Samuels and I are laser focused on ensuring that every student has access to safe and reliable transportation to and from school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It is a core priority of our administration to continue to improve our student transportation systems.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: At New York City Public Schools, we manage the largest and most complex school transportation system in the nation.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: At the same time, we never lose sight of the fact that behind every route, every seat,

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: and every service request a child and family are depending on us.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We know that access to learning starts with students getting to school safely and on time.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I would also like to acknowledge the thousands of bus drivers in attendance, formerly known as matrons, who provide this essential service each and every day.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Many begin their workday as early as 3 and 4 o'clock in the morning to ensure that students arrive safely at school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Their dedication often goes unseen, but it is critical to our success, and we are grateful for everything they do.

chapters.summary: He says NYC operates the largest system in the US, transporting 152,000 students daily with 11,326 buses, 52 companies, 8,850 routes, 9,318 drivers, and 8,849 attendants; over half a million use Omni Transit cards.
chapters.title: Moran details scale of NYC school transportation system

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: New York City operates the largest school transportation system in the United States.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Each day we provide yellow transportation, yellow school bus transportation for about 152,000 students.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Of those, 72,000 students with disabilities are transported from their home to school and back.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: 70,000 travel between stops and school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: 10,000 are pre-K and early intervention students transported directly from their home to school and back.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We achieve those connections with 11,326 school buses across 52 companies,

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: 8,850 routes, 9,318 drivers, 8,849 attendants.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: In addition, over half a million students utilize Omni Transit cards to access public transportation, traveling independently to and from school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Pursuant New York State law, transportation services are provided to eligible students attending public, charter, and non-public schools throughout New York City, as well as students attending specialized programs outside the city when required by their individualized education programs.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: New York City school bus services include students with IEPs, students experiencing homelessness, and students in foster care who have mandated transportation, as well as general education students whose eligibility is based on grade and distance from school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The scale of this operation is unmatched.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And requires daily coordination among schools, families, transportation vendors, city agencies, and our operational teams.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Getting students to school on time and safely is our utmost priority.

chapters.summary: Since January 2024, app usage grew from 1,800 to 10,200 daily average; 80% of users recommend it; student ridership tracking launched spring 2026 with 22,000 parents and full rollout expected spring 2027.
chapters.title: Moran highlights school bus app and ridership tracking

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: While there is more work to be done, I'd like to highlight several areas where we have achieved meaningful progress.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: As it relates to the New York City

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: school bus app.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Beginning in January 2024, in compliance with Local Law 32 of 2019, the New York City school bus has given parents unprecedented visibility into their children's transportation service.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The number of families using the app has grown from a daily average of 1,800 in 2024 to 10,200 this academic year.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We want to continue to encourage families to download and access the app so they can track their students'trips to and from school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Recent survey results show that more than 80% of users would recommend the application to other families.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Families consistently cite real-time tracking and improved communication as key benefits.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We remain confident in the platform and are focused on improving access and training so that more families can fully benefit from the service.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Focused on enhanced ridership tracking.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Beginning in the spring of 26, we launched student ridership tracking capabilities for all New York City school bus umbrella services routes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Through this functionality, families can receive confirmation of when students board and exit their assigned buses, providing additional layer of transparency and peace of mind.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Approximately 22,000 parents have access to ridership tracking, with a full rollout expected by the spring of 27.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Pending the current success of the pilot.

chapters.summary: DOE initiated public vendor report cards with staffing, route performance, safety, and technology compliance; 525,000 students in grades 6-12 have discounted ferry service; digital transit cards are being explored.
chapters.title: Moran describes vendor report cards and expanded transit options

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Vendor report cards.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: This year we initiated public vendor report cards.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: or cards that provide much greater transparency into the transportation company performance.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Families in the public can now review information related to staffing levels, route performance, safety metrics, technology compliance, and service quality indicators.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: This effort reflects our commitment to accountability and transparency,

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: while providing valuable insight into the performance of vendors across our system.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I thank Councilmember Ressler for his legislation, Intro 835, that includes similar oversight requirements.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We look forward to working with you on improving this tool.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Expanded transportation options.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Through our partnership with the Economic Development Corporation, 525,000 students in grades 6 through 12 now have access to discounted New York City ferry service.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We also continue to explore innovative transportation solutions, including initiatives related to the digital transit cards, while working closely with our partners at MTA and technology providers.

chapters.summary: DOE will host its first transportation town hall Dec 1; bus companies are required to engage families twice per school year; nearly 90% of parents reported satisfaction in 2025-26, but he acknowledges remaining challenges.
chapters.title: Moran outlines family engagement and 90% satisfaction

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: As it relates to family engagement, families have consistently told us they need clearer pathways for resolving transportation concerns and connecting directly with bus companies.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So on December 1st, we will host our first transportation town hall to help that need by bringing families and transportation providers together in one place.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: In addition to that requirement for bus companies to engage with families twice per school year was included in our most recent contract extension.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We hope these steps

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: marked the beginning of a more direct and productive model of engagement with families we serve.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And in terms of parent satisfaction, during the 25-26 school year, nearly 90% of parents reported being satisfied with their child's transportation services.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: At the same time, we do not dismiss the concerns of the remaining families who face transportation challenges.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Even if a small percentage of students experience service issues, that still represents thousands of children and families.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Our responsibility is not only to maintain high quality of service for the majority, but also identify and implement sustainable solutions for those who are not receiving the services they need.

chapters.summary: He acknowledges delays and gaps, then explains curb-to-school transportation grew 31% from 54,890 to 71,915 students and required routes grew 17% from 5,771 to 6,770 despite declining enrollment.
chapters.title: Moran cites 31% growth in curb-to-school transportation demand

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: While we are proud of the new family engagement model and the work we are doing to expand transportation options, we fully understand that significant challenges remain.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Too many families have experienced delays, route changes, staffing shortages, or gaps in service.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: When transportation fails, it affects more than a student's commute.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It affects school attendance, student learning, family stability, and a family's ability to get to work.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We take our responsibility to students and families seriously and are committed to continuous improvement.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: To understand today's challenges, it is important to understand how dramatically demand for transportation services has increased, particularly among students receiving curb-to-school transportation.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Over the past four years, the number of students receiving curb-to-school transportation

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: school transportation has increased by 31% from 54,890 students to 71,915 students.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The number of required routes has increased by more than 17% from 5,771 routes to 6,770 routes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The growth has occurred even as overall student enrollment declined.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: In short, the challenge facing us today is meeting the unprecedented growth in demand for some of the most resource-intensive transportations that we provide.

chapters.summary: At the start of the school year providers faced staffing pressures and hundreds of routes lacked drivers; through aggressive hiring and daily adjustments, every route unassigned on the first day now has a driver, and coverage improved.
chapters.title: Moran reports progress on driver shortages and route coverage

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: At the start of the school year, transportation providers face significant staffing and capacity pressures.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: As a result, we struggled to find drivers for hundreds of routes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Through aggressive hiring by our transportation providers, close collaboration between vendors and our teams, and daily operational adjustments, we have made substantial progress.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Every route that was unassigned on the first day of school now has a driver.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Overall service coverage has improved significantly since the opening of school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Transportation remains a dynamic operation.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: New students become eligible every day.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Educational placements change.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Students relocate.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And new routes must continue to be created to meet those needs.

chapters.summary: When yellow bus cannot be established, DOE uses rideshare as a temporary bridge, not a replacement; he acknowledges missed pickups and long rides, thanks staff, and commits to workforce development, technology, transparency, and family engagement.
chapters.title: Moran explains rideshare as temporary bridge and commits to improvement

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: When traditional yellow bus service

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: cannot be established immediately, we utilize alternative transportation options to ensure students can continue attending school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: One of those options is rideshare transportation, which serves as a temporary bridge for students awaiting permanent yellow bus assignments and for students experiencing service interruption related to staffing shortages or other operational disruptions.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It is important to emphasize that rideshare is not intended to be a replacement for yellow bus services.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yellow buses remains our preferred transportation model because they provide consistency and less of a time commitment for families.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: In conclusion, let me be clear.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We recognize the frustration experienced by families whose transportation has not been met.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: For those families, system-wide statistics do not change the reality of a missed pickup.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: A long trip in a bus without air conditioning.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Or uncertainty about how a child will get to school using rideshare when their parents need to get to work.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We fully understand and take those concerns seriously, which is why we are working with families to deliver solutions in real time.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We also recognize the extraordinary effort of our staff across the system, thousands of transportation professionals, school staff, and public servants

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: who work every day to improve the service, add capacity, resolve issues in real time, while maintaining communication with families.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And while we are proud to be making progress in the right direction, we look forward to

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: forward to creating positive change in the months ahead.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The reality is that New York City's transportation system is larger and more complex than ever before.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We believe that an investment in workforce development, modernization of existing technology and expanding use of technology,

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: increasing transparency and maintaining ongoing engagement in families, community stakeholders and our local electeds is essential to build out a stronger and more effective system.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We remain steadfast in our commitment to this critical responsibility to ensuring that every student gets to and from school safely.

chapters.summary: He says Intro 835 would require on-time performance reporting and a public dashboard; DOE supports the intent similar to vendor report cards and looks forward to discussing a feasible timeline.
chapters.title: Moran supports intent of Intro 835 and seeks feasible timeline

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And finally, I will turn to proposed legislation.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Intro 835 would require New York City Public Schools to report a school bus on-time performance and maintain an online public dashboard.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We support the intent of the bill, which shares similar oversight requirements as our vendor's report card.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We look forward to discussing a feasible timeline with the council to ensure we meet the reporting requirements, and we look forward to working with the council on delivering transparency and accountability into our systems.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today, and I look forward to answering your questions.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz notes OPT warned about 200 routes without vendors; asks how many eligible students lacked an assigned route or vendor on the first day. Moran says 928 additional routes were needed and hundreds lacked drivers; Benson says about 2,000 students.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions DOE on unassigned routes at start of school year

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Chancellor.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Before the school started, before school started this year, the Office of Pupil Transportation warned school leaders that about 200 routes may not have a vendor available to operate the route at the start of the school year.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: On the first day of the 26-27 school year,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How many eligible students lacked an assigned route or vendor to operate it?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So, as I mentioned in my testimony, we have seen a significant growth in demand for students.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And as it relates to first day of school, we saw an additional 928 routes needed this school year as compared to last.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So at the end of the vendor pick where we assign all our routes citywide, it was identified that we had hundreds, to your point, of routes that we didn't have a driver.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So how many students lacked the route?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yes, and I will say this.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: As of the August 6th registration deadline, we were able to meet the need.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: For those that we saw come in after the pick, we had alerted families that we didn't have a driver and were provisioning rideshare from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: John Benson here was working with us as we went to set up the rideshare.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So, John, do you have the exact numbers of how many kids we're impacting?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Kevin.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: All my names, John Benson from OPT.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Nice to meet you all.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Nice to be here today.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: It was about 2,000 students heading into the school year that we were.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks if most of the 2,000 students were receiving busing due to IEP-mandated services; Moran confirms.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks whether unassigned students had IEP-mandated busing

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I want to thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I would assume were most of those kids receiving busing due to IEP mandated services?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so based on what you just said, those 2,000 students came as a surprise, like they just got an IEP in August of 2026?

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks if students were surprises; Moran says they registered after the Aug 6 deadline and were not surprises. Dinowitz asks if IEP transportation info is not automatically sent; Moran explains students not placed on a route were notified and given prepaid rideshare.
chapters.title: Dinowitz probes why 2,000 students registered after August deadline

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So when we register all...

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: 150,000 students every year.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We work with schools to put them in our systems.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so they weren't a surprise.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: They were registered after the August 6th deadline.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The state of New York sets a benchmark of...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Sorry, let me back up.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Explain this to me.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This is how it goes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A special education teacher and a family will write an IEP, and it will say student needs transportation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And you're saying that you have to register that information separately that does not get automatically sent to you on a computer?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It does get sent to us.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So for those who didn't register, it doesn't get sent to us.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So we have 3,000 schools and programs that we support.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: What happened between the time of registration and the time of first day of school, there were students that were not placed on a route.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The moment after the vendor pick where we assign all the routes, we saw those students as not having a route.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We notified the schools, we notified the families, and we gave a prepaid ride share and saying, we're going to work to put you on.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It wasn't a surprise.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I don't mean to, I want to understand what you mean by registered.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Registered for school at all or had an IEP?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What do you mean by they registered after that deadline?

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks for clarification on what 'registered' means; Moran says it could be new admits, new IEPs, change of school or address, or IEP provision changes like travel time. Dinowitz presses whether all changes happened after the deadline; Moran says yes, could be a new admit or change of school.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks Moran to explain registration and IEP changes

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yes, they actually entered a request for school bus transportation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So explain this to me as if I don't know anything about busing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: These are students who are already registered for school, correct?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: These could be new admits.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: These could be new IEPs.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: They could be change of school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: This could be change of address.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Right, but that's what I'm asking is they already have IEPs, and what you're saying is all 2,000 kids either registered for school to enter,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: a school after that August deadline, or they only got their IEP after August?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It's not as simple as they didn't just get their IEP.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It's a combination.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That is a grouping of students that for whatever the reason, it could have been an IEP existing, but the IEP provision changed.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I needed rather than limited time travel at 60 minutes, I needed it at 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That route changed.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But what you're saying is all of those changes happened after

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The August deadline, every single one of them?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It could be a new admit.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It could be a change of school.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about driver shortages and retention; DOE describes aggressive hiring and daily operational adjustments to cover routes.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer questions DOE on bus driver hiring and retention

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It could be a change of program.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It could be a parent change of dress.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: When we route, we route on information provided across our 3,000 schools and programs.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: They provide information in our source system.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That information is sent to us in real time, and then we route accordingly.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Straight from CESIS, it gets to you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Well, CESIS, it could now, by the way, I would say this, you may remember ATS, your time at teaching.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I think my grandfather's grandfather remembers ATS.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The good news is OPT is the largest division in the agency that has fully migrated into NOAA's platform.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So we get data in much better timelines, and it helps us on all the routing platforms for all the students.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So I would say we get the information as fast as we can from schools.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: There's no delay, and we start routing accordingly.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And how many eligible students remain without bus service as of today?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So I can take you through the crosswalk.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So at current.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We're looking at, there are, as we look at the top line, there are

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: 467 students total as it relates to the 150,000 that we serve.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I will say that- That don't have bus routes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So we had in the last five days, nearly 250 students routed.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: In the last six to 10 days, we have just slightly under 50 students registered.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And then the remaining, we have roughly 31 students in the 11 to 15 band.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, and I'm going to ignore it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They have routes, although, as we discussed briefly before the hearing, some of those routes may be inefficient.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I was sharing a story about a constituent of mine who was offered a bus route to pick their child up at 3.30.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Their school ends at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So the choice that this parent has to make...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is do I take my child out of school an hour early, a child with a disability who needs that support and education, or do we pay for private transport?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And these are the decisions that although they may be assigned a bus route, these are still the decisions families are left to contend with.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We regret that the session time doesn't align in this instance.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Years back, OPT would schedule session times across the industry.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Right now,

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: School leaders suggest a session time for every school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We do our very best to work with schools on getting the right session time for every school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So if there's a specific example, John and I can definitely look at scheduling that properly.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Now, I mean, the whole point is that there are specific examples.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Each one of us can think of half a dozen from the past few weeks who've emailed our office.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think the point is the systemic changes that we need to see in the Office of People Transportation, in the buses, in the contracts, and in the entire system.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Of the children who are now arriving to school late or parents who do choose to have their kids leave school early so that they can make the bus,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: how many students have received makeup instruction or related services for time lost to bus failures in 2026-2027?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And how does the DOE identify those still owed services?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So just to go back to the session time, I think it's important to realize that we'll work with any school or provider on making those adjustments.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We receive session times from school leaders and superintendents across the school system, and then we map to that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So if there's a time that doesn't work for a school, John and I need to know about that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We need to make that adjustment.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So to the family impacted there, we regret that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That is a follow-up for me to take back.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: As it relates to make-up services, John Hammer, you want to take it?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: John Hammer, the Chief of the Division of Inclusive and Accessible Learning.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: We know how critical it is that students receive their specialized instruction and mandated services that are outlined on their IEPs.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: You know, our schools are equipped to work with families and students to kind of assess any impact that a delay of school bus transportation is impacting access to services.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Families should and do regularly have conversations with principals around how we might be able to move around,

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: change the time that students are receiving speech, occupational therapy, physical therapy, to limit any impact of a school bus delay.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And we will be working over the course of the school year through annual review IEP meetings to assess any impact of lost instruction and to ensure that kids receive what they need.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think it feels like you're talking about a good idea, but when you're a child in a school and you have to get your math, you gotta get your ELA, gotta get your luncheon, you're talking about taking kids

chapters.summary: A parent testifies that their child's bus arrived an hour late, causing the child to miss breakfast and morning instruction, and asks for better communication.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: if they even have the time in school, taking them out of their gym class, taking them out of their art class, sometimes the very things that are most important for our kids with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And that's completely ignoring the fact that our buses don't allow for after-school programs.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So even in the instance where a kid wanted to stay after school to make up the services, the contracts and the routes are so rigid as to not allow for students to stay after school to get their services.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I do want to talk about the routes and tracking though.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to talk about Via.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You've heard of this Via?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I heard some groans from the people in the gallery.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think you know why you heard groans, and even from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The city bought four things.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Tracking, one, tracking buses.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Two, tracking students as they board an exit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Three, optimizing routes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And four, turn-by-turn navigation for drivers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All those were due by the end of 2021.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So I would say that expectations and our current state dictate when these are due.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think if you look at the timeline of when the VIA contract was awarded in response to local laws 32, 33, and 34, and to which they are, we started implementation in 2020.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And I will be honest with you, COVID completely interrupted what exactly we were doing on infrastructure development, our OPT modernization, and actually paying the vendor.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So development did stop.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We were focused on contact tracing at the time, and John and I were in the situation room looking at COVID cases and coming out of COVID.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I will tell you the priority at the time was not developing fully the VIA system.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I will say this.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: What VIA does for us is what we ask.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And I will say specifically, we did

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: not ask for these things to be developed at the cadence that would be commiserate with the timeline you just shared.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We were not ready.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You didn't ask for it to be, they weren't due by the end of 2021?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We were not ready to advance into those platforms through our own integration of systems.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So it wasn't that VIA was noncompliant.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It was we were not ready to move in, whether we did not have the business rules developed, the systems development ready to move.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So the system wasn't moving at a pace to suggest we could meet that deadline.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's surprising here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's been seven years, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: COVID happened, and that impacted all of us, and it impacted operations.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But we've been out of COVID for a while, and kids have been going to school in person since, I guess, 2021 or 2020, right?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We've had the vaccine since 2021.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so it's a little surprising to hear that it wasn't, these weren't priorities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's been seven years since the contract.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it seems that we're willing to pay $36 million for I don't know what, for routes that are still problematic.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we'll talk about the routes in a second, but please respond.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah, so there is a lot that's developed thus far.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think what is remaining ultimately is the routing optimization.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: All other items have been completed.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So parents can log into the New York City School Bus app now and see it.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Parents can actually enjoy the ridership tracking and see when students get on and when they get off.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The pilot was successful.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think when you look at it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I do want to pause you there.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Because I think some of the riders and the parents will say it wasn't successful.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, if this is the app you're talking about, only an 80% satisfaction rate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I will note that drivers have trouble logging in.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They've had to take screenshots to prove that they logged in.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: When there are half days, the bus company doesn't believe them that they logged in because it was a half day in the middle.
