utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could we see an expansion of the nice bus model in this next contract as a reasonable expectation?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think it's reasonable to expect expansion.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think they have demonstrated an ability to perform the work.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And certainly we'll look to them to continue to grow.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: As shortages arise, my expectation, and I think these conversations I had, are that they assume those routes where other companies cannot.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so they do have a training program that I'm encouraged by that I want to learn more about.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so, yes, I would say expanding is absolutely an option.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I'm going to just do one last question.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: An audit by the Comptroller's Office found in FY 23-24, in school year 23-24, there were over 15,000 complaints about

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: late pickups and arrivals, 16,000 complaints about special education transportation, 14,000 no-show complaints, 5,000 reports of disconnected calls.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you just help me understand when a parent has an issue, what's the best case scenario for the process when they have an issue with their bus?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is it that they should be calling the transportation coordinator at their school to work through issues?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that data publicly accessible?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you have confidence that parents know who their transportation coordinators are?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They know who the points of contact are?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How do we and how do you kind of analyze and look at repeat issues when we have chronic problems to make sure they're being addressed?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So just what's the best case scenario for how issues are being addressed?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are transportation coordinators the solution?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How do we do a better job of making their information available, accessible publicly to all parents and encouraging them to reach out?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And then how are you addressing chronic and repeat issues?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That's a great question, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And aligned in many ways to Member Brewer's commentary about how do we make sure families have a unified experience.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think much of this can be associated with the New York City School Bus app where we simply contact us, and that is merging.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: To change the experience, to your point, if you call a transportation liaison and they're working on an issue in a school, working closely, that's not tracked or evaluated either.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So I think we have to change the customer experience.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so I'm excited about some of the work we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We have a lot of work we could do to kind of automate this.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We do have an online platform, too, where you don't have to call or wait online, although we're proud of the response times and the recovery we made in the call center.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: But this is overdue in terms of having a different platform for parents to resolve issues.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And I've heard from some and saying, look, I don't want to just be given a number.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And then they say thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so we want to be more.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Interactive with families on resolutions too.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks about the timeline for rebidding school bus contracts; DOE says a full rebid takes about 18 months and that planning is underway.
chapters.title: Council Member De La Rosa questions DOE on contract rebid timeline

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So we just

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We just don't want to track a call.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We want to make sure that we solve a problem.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If you don't have that app, what would you recommend to a parent?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: First step would be the transportation liaison at the school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think, like most services connected to student at school, the school leadership team there and the staff are there.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: They're the most welcoming, affirming front line we have, and thank you to all the school administrators and school support staff that take care of our busing apparatus each and every morning reporting to us.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We need to do a better job of having a platform.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And should their information be listed on the school's website so people know who had to reach them?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Let's take that back.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, that's an idea under consideration.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're brainstorming ways to do that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We need to know clearly who the individuals are, and then we can work on posting.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There's other issues we have to work through to do that, but we're committed to doing it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Chair Dinowitz, thank you for your latitude.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm shutting up.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Every time.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm a little surprised by your last answer.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're looking for ways to do that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's a website, and it's 2026.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It just feels like it's an easy thing for you to say yes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're going to put the transportation coordinator's name and contact info on the website.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's a very easy thing to say yes at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We want to make sure we engage fully staff, I think, putting people's contact information, whether or not.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think we also need a coherence around.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's not their personal cell phone number.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I want to make sure there's coherence around who's identified as a transportation coordinator insofar as they're not teaching math, period one.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: or their parent coordinator and their meeting with families at period two.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think we need to think about this because I don't want the experience to be, I contact that person, you said, and they're just not available.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Maybe they're doing cafeteria coverage or something.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Let me come back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think we need to have a good conversation about transportation coordinators, which we will in a second.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We have not received either from CLA or the DOE a response to the clarifying email that we sent out.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I guess we're getting it right now, allegedly.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Allegedly.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: He's not under oath, so I'm not sure if that's true.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The transportation coordinator, can you describe, is this a full-time job at a school, or is this a job whose tasks are just added to another employee's plate?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Well, first, we want to make sure a school has an individual that can...

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: one, access OPT, and two, escalate issues within their district, within OPT to resolve.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think the position may need more time in development, but John, I don't want to talk about exactly the role.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: So the expectation is every school has a dedicated transportation coordinator.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: It is not a staff position.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: A school doesn't hire a transportation coordinator specifically.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: It's work that's assigned by a principal to someone that works in the school.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Could be the parent coordinator, could be an AP, could be a dean, could be a teacher.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: And that varies across 3,000 plus schools.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: So capturing all of that becomes a challenge.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Like who are the people in each school?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: What is their contact information?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Do they have you?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: union concerns we have to work through before we put these things online.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Those are all the issues we need to work through before we can do it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, I mean, but it's been this way for years, and I think families have been asking who's the dedicated transportation coordinator, who they don't know on the website.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That would have been an easy yes for you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But it seems that, let's say, if they're a teacher, they're teaching their five classes, they got their prep, they got their lunch, they got the professional assignment, where would the time be?

chapters.summary: A shelter-based advocate testifies that students in temporary housing face frequent bus route changes and lack of communication, disrupting attendance.
chapters.title: Public witness describes bus service for homeless students

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is there a regulation that it would have to be a release period?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I've heard that it could be a school aide who's already assigned to, you know, maybe collecting cell phones at the beginning of the day, monitoring the halls.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's just an extra task assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I've heard you've mentioned it could be the parent coordinator who's, as you acknowledge, already dealing with parent phone calls, not just for transportation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It could be an assistant principal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And as we know from these hearings, assistant principals also have to sometimes work as school safety agents because we also don't have enough school safety agents.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, so what is your vision for what a transportation coordinator looks like at a school?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it varies on scale and scope.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think there are some schools that don't rely on yellow bus service.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think there's some that have 50 buses outside their building.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So let me come back to you on what that could look like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What's your vision for it?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What would you like to see?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Well, I mean, an individual that did have that capacity, that bandwidth to deal with, look, the reality is I don't want to have escalations coming in every day, all day.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so this shouldn't be a massive.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: You know, workflow, but I do see campuses with 50 buses lined up outside, and I do know that's a lot.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We manage on any

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: given day, 300,000 unique student experiences.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So let's, I mean, is there some sort of threshold?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like if there are 20 buses lined up outside of school, should that school have a dedicated transportation coordinator?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah, so it's on paper.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I hear you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I understand it.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: But let me come back to you on what that could look as a system.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Because right now we ask that a person is designated, like other positions to your point, and we want to have a name, so to speak, as who's the person that a parent could go to.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So we'll find it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, you have to understand there's a difference between some of the...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Positions that are designated like a sustainability coordinator, which is they're assigned and maybe they do stuff and maybe they don't and it's based on their bandwidth, but we can't leave transportation

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: up to the professionals'bandwidth that they happen to have.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Just because it's mandated to have a transportation coordinator.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This is a real job, and parents need to be able to reach out to them any time they need them related to transportation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so I think the conversation is more, when you have 20 buses at a school, shouldn't the DOE pay for a person whose job it is to be transportation coordinator?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Point well taken.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We will follow up.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I do appreciate that commentary.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I do know we have borough liaisons that I think John and I, we should talk about posting as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: But school specific, I'm going to have to come back to you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And on your end, what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Which department in the Department of Education does it require you to have those meetings?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Well, we have borough liaisons in each borough, so we cover the whole city that report to OPT.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But you don't have, you know, when it comes to...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: to the budgeting of schools, is that also your department?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So that's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Which department in the Department of Education will you be discussing about getting some of those line items for some of the schools that have the most complicated cases to have a dedicated transportation coordinator or the release time and the training?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll talk to our leadership team about

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: All of the work that happens at a school level, our schools supported in the work they have to do inclusive of transportation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So the leadership team, that's the...

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's the department?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Council Member Joseph?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Wanted to talk about a report in July of 2026, 1,775 students in temporary housing were waiting to be routed.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: On average, how many days after move until a student in temporary housing has bus services?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And also, same question applied for our students in foster care.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So first of all, thank you for your advocacy.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how DOE engages parents in transportation planning; DOE cites town halls and bus company requirements but acknowledges parents are not included in route decisions.
chapters.title: Council Member Gutiérrez questions DOE on parent engagement

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: This is work that this administration takes very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We have been part of daily busing sinks with this administration and the chancellor.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And I could say we asked down to the individual student.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: In this administration.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And it's work we've been doing, it's work we're proud of.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And as it relates to, just as we look at right now, as it relates to foster care as well, I know every given night, and this is last night, so far there's 1,059

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Foster students all routed and we have four waiting to be routed and they were all added students added in the last five days.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: As it relates to students in temporary housing, it's another data set we look at nightly and we want to make sure every student, and I want to thank our partners at DHS and I want to thank the partners on our team that lead this work.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Deputy Chancellor Flavia Pueblo-Podemo, for all her leadership in this space, we have right now all 4,931 students routed.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: In the last five days, we added 52, so we have to add 52.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: In the last six to 10 period, we had 10 students added.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We have 62 in the normal kind of waiting to be routed, 62 students out of the 4,931.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And then we have two students in between 11 to 15 and a single student at 16 to 20.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Now, we're looking at this nightly, and so that's the precision.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We have a team that evaluates this work, and I'd introduce Famida Salim, who does this work in partnership.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: With our SDH team at Central.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So, Famida, if you would just take a bit on process.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think we have to swear you in also.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee, and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There you go.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: Samita Salim.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: Thank you so much for that question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: The process for a student residing in DHS shelter is very, very simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: We recognize that we want to make it very simple for families so they can connect with their DHS caseworker at the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: The caseworker will then update their preference in the DHS CARES system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: We receive that data daily, and based on that, we can set up transportation very quickly.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm happy that at least two agencies are talking, DHS and New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That's a rare, that's very rare in this space.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What about our students in foster care?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Normally, I have about 1,271.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How long is the average wait time for our students in foster care and temporary housing, students in temporary housing to get a route?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: Student in foster care is a great priority for us and especially for my team as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: Oh, I know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: Five to seven days right now is how much we use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: As long as the foster care agencies have notified the school, the address has been updated, and we receive an exception request.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: Right now, I only have two pending applications.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Just two waiting to get placed in a route?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Famida Salim
utterances.text: Two, and we received four new ones that just came in.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay, well, I'll keep looking.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In 2027, I was advocating for $3 million for our students for interim transportation for students in foster care, but it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I'm looking to see, will that be included in fiscal 2028?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is that something we plan to fight for?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: For that, we'll come back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We'll follow up for sure.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: But I want to say one of the things I remember you advocating for was the reimbursement to the ACS providers as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I'm happy to report that program was completely revamped, and we have no outstanding debt, if you will, to reimbursements of agency providers that are providing services for transportation.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And it takes long to reimburse agencies.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We also cripple them as small agencies that are doing the most for our most vulnerable students in this system.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I will definitely continue to monitor that unique population.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you for all that you do.

chapters.summary: A charter school parent testifies that bus service is inconsistent and that charter students are often left out of route planning and communication.
chapters.title: Public witness describes bus service for charter school students

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: In my district, I notice a lot of buses that do pickups across boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And I have seen, I've spoken to bus drivers that, oh, I have to do another pickup in Brooklyn, not just...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The other side of the border, like really further down.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my question is that how many of these routes do you have that serve as multiple boroughs?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And do you have plans to reduce these routes?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because they take a long time and it gives a great strain.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: For the child to sit there for

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: for extended periods of time.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah, and that's a great question and commentary because it's one of our focuses is to make sure we reduce distance and time travel.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We do have a lot of out-of-borough routes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We do have students traveling through multiple boroughs to get to school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And as John Hammer had mentioned earlier, we're doing our very best to move program closer to home and so that we can reduce those lengthy commutes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I don't know, John, if you have the out-of-borough spreadsheet available.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: John, do you have a count on how many?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We have out of borough.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I don't know if you have that with you.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: I'll circle back with you on out-of-borough routes, but it is quite a few, and that's largely based on where the student resides and where they attend school.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: It's not something we actively elect to do.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: We bring students from where they live to school, regardless of where those locations are.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: They could be in different boroughs, and in that case, it results in an inter-borough route.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And that's by close of business we can get to you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We have the chart.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I just don't have it.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I also did some research about the vendor NYC School Bus Umbrella Services.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And it seemed to me that the cost per child on that contract is considerably more than your average contractor.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Do you agree to my...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: computations, numbers?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation why it costs so much more?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: There's a couple of variables there.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: NiceBus does have

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: the contract with the ATU, so there are employee protection provisions.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So those are labor costs, there are pension costs, there are medical costs.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: NiceBus currently does not own property, own real property, and so we're leasing across that portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So I think there is a disadvantage in that space as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: But I think largely it's largely wages and lease payments.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: There's one case that my office is currently working on, which the child, there's a child that he is given that he will board the bus for 625 and drop off at 815.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But if you look at it, he's spending, what is it?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: hour, hour and a half each way on the bus, which seems to be, that exceeds

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: the DOE's a lot of time because there's a maximum time that you set up that's only that the child can only, should sit in the bus for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What is being done?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or do you keep track of these issues?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because the parents is telling me that the child is very stressful, spending one and a half hour each day, or sometimes an hour and 45 minutes to get to school and then come back from school.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What's being done to fix that?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: C is important, and distance and time travel is equally as important.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think Councilmember Ressler's bill is going to provide a greater level of transparency.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We're working until that ends with our vendor report card as well, because I think distance time traveled matters, and I think the ridership tracking is going to be the tool that tells us

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: when Kevin boarded bus and when Kevin exited bus, and to work at the data analysis in a way that would change a route quicker than traditionally has done.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So in particular, in this route, we can definitely connect with our team and see what we can do.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks about electric school buses and emissions; DOE says it is exploring electric buses but has no firm timeline for fleet transition.
chapters.title: Council Member Krishnan questions DOE on bus emissions and electric buses

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: This is very concerning to me because the child has an IEP and has special needs, and that's why I'm bringing it up to you now.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And then I think we can do better on keeping track of these routes that extends beyond the maximum time spent in the bus.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And then we need to look at the child and see what we can do to reduce that time.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And in any case that you or any council members share with our IGA team, with our team here, we're happy to look into and come back in real time with an assessment and an update.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do I have time for one more?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: You do?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Those dings in the beginning were not for you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: How many complaints you get on an average day from parents?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah, so the complaint center, as someone who in September 2018 was asked to help, we had over 150,000 calls in the month of September.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We don't see that in a school year.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: But specific to your question, on average now, we manage 300,000 unique experiences.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We have about 400 to 500 complaints in our call center on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Lower on Fridays.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Is that been increasing steadily or that's been always the case?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: No, it's down significantly.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Down.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Finish up your last question.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: But what about calls that, is that directly to DOE?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: What about like calls to 311 or calls to the bus company?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Do you have those figures or they're not included in the figures you just said?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So any call that comes into the call center, we track, manage, and evaluate.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so those are captured and we have real-time data and analytics.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I'm happy to share any part of that because it's pretty impressive.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Our call turnaround time is improved, the response rates, there's no wait times.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So we're real proud of our call center.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: If a call does come via 311, I don't know, John, if we don't roll that into the call center itself.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: We would not roll the 311 call into our call center statistics themselves.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Those issues are flagged by the 311 team to us, and we do investigate and follow up and resolve to the extent we can, but it's not factored.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: into our call center stats.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You don't keep track of calls calling directly to the bus company either, right?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a very good point.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It's to the point of Member Brewer that we believe that a unified call center would help us better manage the calls to the companies and the calls to OPT.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So we're coming back on that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairman.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In the spring, the Department of Education recognized $27.9 million in savings in fiscal year 27 budget for route efficiencies.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can you please explain how the DOE is realizing these savings and if the DOE is on track to achieve those savings in the current fiscal year?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So, excellent question.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Before the question, is it okay if John shares the out-of-borough rundown real quick?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This is in response to Councilor Wong's question.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Yes, so routes traveling between boroughs, that is 2,699 routes encompassing over 10,000 students.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: 2,699 school bus routes with a total of over 10,000 students on those routes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So as it relates to route.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And how many of them are generally on time or many like?

chapters.summary: A parent in temporary housing testifies that their child's bus route changed three times in one month, causing missed school and stress.
chapters.title: Public witness describes bus service for students in temporary housing

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Are they late all the time?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: I would say the majority of them arrive on time, and then there are routes that struggle.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: And concrete data on that I don't have in front of me, but we can get you that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Joe.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So to the question on route optimization, I think the monies that we intended to see through routing with the influx of students

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: to answer your question directly, I don't think we'll see those cost savings only because we added year over year 928 new routes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So I don't think, I think the premise of the route inefficiency, we lost that in terms of the growth.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We're adding routes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We're not sitting.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I, we, so we can also assume the $55.9 million in savings from route efficiencies and fiscal 28 will not materialize.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The trend in the growth, we would not realize that, that savings.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Does the DOE believe the 2.28 billion fiscal 2027 budget for people transportation

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: contracts is correct or will additional funding be needed in future financial plan?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And if the amount is under budgeted, why?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We feel it's correct.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Feels correct.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think it's worth pointing out, you know, I mentioned this

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: student of mine who has to choose, the family has to choose between leaving school early and paying for bus service.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This is one of the students, like I think Councilmember Brewer was saying, this is one of the students who sued the DOE.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: To get free and appropriate public education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And this is a student who wanted to be in public school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the mom was begging to be in public school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They held IEP meetings without her.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They took away this kid's IEP.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They did all sorts of things that were inviting a lawsuit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They were like asking for a lawsuit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And this is the story of so many families throughout the city that want to be in our public school system, but because of missteps by the DOE or the inability to service those students in their home district,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: despite their desires, feel the need to sue the Department of Education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: From your perspective, from the Office of People Transportation, what conversations do you have with leadership

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and with other offices to reduce the number of due process claims and cases, thereby negating the need for children to travel, at least some of them, to travel to far-flung places in our city?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It's an excellent question.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: As a New York City public school parent for three kids in the system at one point in time and ultimately starting as a classroom teacher.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: in a self-contained environment.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I remember vividly parents and students'reliance on transportation just to meet the day and get to and from school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think we need to do a better job of amplifying our quality programs and matching that commiserate with quality transportation.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I regret hearing the story about a session time and a family having to choose.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That should not be the place we put parents.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: They should not have to choose.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We should do a better job on matching our session time and route time, and that's something I'm committed to.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: In this specific instance or any instance that comes up, it's a conversation I have actively with superintendents and principals about making sure the time works for families as well, both co-located schools.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, I know to your credit, you, Deputy Chancellor, are very responsive to individual needs, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But these needs should not arise to the extent at which they do.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so my question is, what advocacy are you doing within the Department of Education and to OMB

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: to say, look, we're spending a lot on transportation, we have a lot of late routes, we'd like to reduce the number of students who need to go to all sorts of places in the city.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And therefore advocating to OMB and within the DOE for more of those programs, whether it's District 75 or related services,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: that meet the needs of students closer to home.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What does your advocacy look like there?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it's an excellent question, and so thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It's something I'm in lockstep with Deputy Chancellor Fodion around inclusive environments.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And again, I said I was in a self-contained classroom and I felt there's such a need for kids to be seen in their own community and affirmed on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think our advocacy is about quality program.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And I think John Hammer shared about that earlier about the things they're doing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And for us, I think one of the areas in transportation is looking at.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Transportation not only as a service, but as something that is on the least restrictive environment continuum.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Whereas if you start in age four in a smaller vehicle and graduate at age 22 in that same vehicle, we really missed the mark in providing you with a least restrictive environment.

chapters.summary: Louis asks about training for bus attendants and matrons; DOE describes training requirements and says it is working to improve consistency.
chapters.title: Council Member Louis questions DOE on bus attendant training

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so things we talk about around travel training, independence, the appropriateness of service.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think there's so much in that space on the continuum where we can find value for students and, you know, ultimately provide different opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so, John, I don't know if you want to add a little bit more about the expanding programs, but I think that's.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The bottom line for us is quality programs close to home.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So to John.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Yeah, this is an area where Deputy Chancellor Moran and his team have been great partners to us.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Looking at our current travel training program, which is operated out of the District 75 team office of travel training and trying to think a little bit more expansively around how we can build out supports.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Just a couple years ago, we launched a program called Journey to Independence alongside, you know, through many conversations.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: with the Office of Pupil Transportation in order to really build pre-travel training skills and bring families alongside to say what are the skills that a child would need in order to be able to travel more independently.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And so that is one example of a new program that has launched over the last couple of years through close partnership with our Office of Pupil Transportation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm really glad you brought up some of, you know, viewing this as a service, least restrictive environment, a fellow self-contained teacher,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: something I think both you and I understand very deeply by giving students the tools they need to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You've seen an IEP before.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You've seen CSIS before.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Describe the page that talks about student transportation.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah, there's very little in the way of choice.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so essentially, you have a choice if you want transportation just to check that you want door-to-door.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: John, I don't know if you want to add.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think that covers it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So does that lend itself well to having these conversations?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Does it lend itself well to saying you want transportation or not?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: To discussing things like travel training, does it lend itself well to those conversations?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And we have an obligation to do better.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think providing a full range of options.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So whereas Kevin at age 13 could consider one method or at age 14, another, maybe 16, another.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So we'll come back to you on some concrete recommendations in terms of how we work with schools to fully illustrate a range of options versus

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: If you have an IEP, you only get door-to-door service.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So we do.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, you can come back to me, which is necessary.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But I think it's also important you go to the office for students with disabilities and talk to them about what the training looks like and what the IEP looks like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Because the questions that are asked on the IEP drive the conversation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So is it your opinion then that we should have check boxes or questions asked that are a little more detailed than simply transportation, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so can we look forward to...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: hearing a report from your conversation, not just with leadership, but the Office of Students with Disabilities, to update that page and to update the training that's provided to IEP teachers?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I will absolutely come back to you with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Yeah, this is a topic that we've been in communication, actually, with OPT and the Division of Operations about, and it's something that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, obviously your work isn't just busing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's deeply intertwined to the IEP and to the work of so many other...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: People in the Department of Education, both on the ground and in Central.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Speaking of the travel training, I know this is something you value very much.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We've spoken about this.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You mentioned it just now in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But it has been reported to me that if you seek travel training, you are then no longer eligible for the school bus.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So one of the considerations we heard early is what is that flexible program?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: What could it look like?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And I understand, I think, John, the feedback we've gotten thus far was this should be time-bound.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And it's under consideration.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: By time-bound, I mean if you're entering into a travel training program, you still maintain eligibility for a six-month period while you work towards independence.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So that's a takeaway.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That's a concrete piece of feedback.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It's legitimate feedback we need to consider.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so we'll come back on a decision.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: But we think maintaining dual eligibility through the travel training process would encourage more families to participate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You feel that way, but what is a timeline on that?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can we expect it to be implemented?

chapters.summary: A non-public school parent testifies that bus service is unreliable and that communication with OPT is difficult, forcing families to arrange private transportation.
chapters.title: Public witness describes bus service for non-public school students

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What would it take to implement that?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It's early in discussion, so that is a team takeaway.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We will absolutely come back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so it would mean necessarily that a student is eligible for the yellow bus and is getting an Omni card, correct?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That's also the idea is like to figure out, is there, so

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: in part, yes, they would carry eligibility in both through a sequence and then reevaluate at a set date by family, set date in a, to your point that

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: the IEP would have measurable goals like anything else and say we would look at this.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And then at that point, would we, one, go straight to Omni if travel training and independence has been achieved, or two, maintain, or three, you know, to create the program.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, and that goes back to the IEP.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There are annual, there's an annual goal section.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Typically, I think in many cases, it's academic.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But there are also annual goals for traveling and travel training.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I think we all want our children to be able to.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Travel as independently as possible.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So those are critical annual goals and it needs to be supported.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the structures need to be there by your office to allow for that to happen.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Yeah, I would just say that you're hitting on a very important point.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Came into the hearing today and saw some folks standing outside.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: I did see a young man with the sign expand travel training and it's not uncommon for our students to be very clear with us around where we need to focus our efforts and attention.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: We also repeatedly hear from students, families, schools that the largest barrier to adult independence for our students with disabilities is an inability to travel independently to employment, to higher education, day habilitation programming.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And so we have, you know, we are working, you know, to strengthen our travel training work, both through new programs, as I spoke about earlier around Journey to Independence.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: We're also looking at capacity within our current team of travel trainers within District 75.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And really prioritizing our pre-employment transition service contract, our pre-ETS contract,

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: which funding that we received from the state to build travel training into really our workplace readiness training that comes through pre-ETS.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And so excited that we're going to be adding additional travel trainers in the winter to support this work through our pre-ETS grant.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And we're always looking at ways to expand this program.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is there a waiting list for students and families seeking travel training?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: There are around 200 students that are awaiting travel training right now.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And will the DLE be making a budget request?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: We're excited that we're expanding the team by five, and we're seeking funding through private entities, through the Fund for Public Schools, something that we've been talking to folks about.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is five sufficient for that wait list?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: You know, to each trainer supports somewhere between 12 and 17 students to take them through the full process and get them to graduate from the program.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And so it's a little short.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, five times 12, 60, right?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So you said it's between 12 and 17.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Students that they support, so 200 students on the wait list and probably need somewhere around 12 to 15 staff to meet that full need.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That sounds like the math.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And that's a request that you'll be making.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I recall last...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Budget cycle, it was actually one of the proposed cuts by the administration.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It was proposed that they cut travel training in addition to a litany of other things in our schools, but that was specifically targeted for cuts.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Will the administration be requesting more funding for more positions, for more travel training?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: We're always looking at ways to expand our travel training unit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do I have to request it?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Will you be required?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You have these conversations, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: We will be working with...

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: and our leadership team to determine priorities for the agency and requesting funds from OMB as the budget cycle.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, so it's clear the DOE wants it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So let's see in the preliminary budget if it is proposed to once again cut the travel training or if it'll be enhanced, which is kind of what you're testifying that our students and families want.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They want independence.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They want it before they graduate from high school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, this would be a huge win to get our kids a little more independence in transit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, I want to talk about the cost per route and students.

chapters.summary: Farías asks about specific bus delays in the Bronx; DOE acknowledges challenges and describes route adjustments and driver hiring.
chapters.title: Council Member Farías questions DOE on bus service in the Bronx

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: According to the controller in fiscal 2024, DOE spent $21,719 per student on curb to school service.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And 6,761 per student on stop to school service.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The DOE disputed the stop to school figure and put it at about 4,900 per student.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What was the average cost per curb to school route in fiscal 2026?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And what were the highest and lowest route costs?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So the cost per student analysis is something we focus on, and so our budget team is looking at, but it varies between individuals.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so there are settings by which we have, even in the stop-to-school environment, it will vary.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Some routes on a stop-to-school could have 14 kids.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Some could have 50 kids.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So the routes vary.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I would say on the curb-to-school, it varies based on IEP need.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Some have driver, attendant, para, or multiple paras, and or nurse.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So the cost does vary.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I don't know, John, if you have the latest numbers you could share here.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: For curb to school routes, the average cost per route is $239,036.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That's the average cost?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And what would that be on the low end and high end?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: I don't have the low end and high end, but it's going to be a small range above or below.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: I don't have the exact range.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Within like a few thousand, 10,000?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's a reasonable assumption, yes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So, okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So you'll get back to us with that exact figure, please.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: What was the average cost per stop to school?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: To stop to school route in fiscal 26, and what were the lowest and highest drought costs?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: So I have fiscal 27 in front of me for both service categories.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: I don't have 20.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: 26 in front of me, but for this year, it's $176,253 average for stop to school route.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: For stop to school, okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And how does the DOE calculate the cost of each type route, each type of route?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It's a combination of staffing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So it's the numbers of staff on each individual route.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And you consider paraprofessionals and nurses as part of the cost?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's separate cost.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Those will actually, the attendant cost and the driver cost directly.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Those are separate and apart.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can you walk us through why curb-to-school routes are more expensive?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is it the route length?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is it the staffing, the vehicle type, or something else?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Off the jump, it's two staff members per route versus one staff member.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What are the two staff members per curb?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: For a curb, you have a driver and attendant in each and every circumstance.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And in a stop to school, you only have a driver?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Solely the bus driver.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Solely the driver.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: On a curb-to-school route, how much of the cost is fixed and how much changes with the number of riders?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That is actually fixed.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It's a contract item that they select, and it's set.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Actually, in the item, the cost is set, and they actually select that cost.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: By the route?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But no matter how many kids are on that route.

chapters.summary: A parent of a student with mobility disabilities testifies that the bus lacks proper restraints and that drivers are not trained to secure wheelchairs safely.
chapters.title: Public witness describes bus service for students with mobility disabilities

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah, we see that variation in our pre-K contracts, which allow per pupil cost.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And just going back to the, I know, I think it was Councilmember Narcisse asked about the nurses, but do you have a sense of, do you have data on how many

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: students are not getting their busing because they require a para during transit?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So that is something we evaluate.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: You know, a provision of our ride share does allow for ride share provision for a driver being absent in a curb to school environment in terms of a power being absent or a power yet to be hired.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So, John, we do track that number.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I don't know if you have the latest today.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a very important question.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: It's important not only that students are routed timely, but they have the supports that they need to ride the school bus safely.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: In total, there's around 4,300, just over 4,300 students that have a mandate for a bus power professional.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And we're working to assign just over 350 of those students an IEP bus power professional currently.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There are how many students without the bus power?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: We are in the process of arranging bus power professional services for a little over 350 students currently.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Those students have been offered ride share to Deputy Chancellor Moran's point earlier.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: We're also offering...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The ride share requires the parent to travel with them.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: A parent is able to designate anybody over the age of...

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: 18 to ride with the child.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: So yes, it's not a perfect solution and it does not work for everyone.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: But there's been a lot of conversations with OPT around how to make it the most accessible that we can make it.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: We also provide travel reimbursement of funding for families that can leverage that and know that we have to do better in ensuring that every child receives.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's, you know, again, it's very troubling.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I know we have the parish shortages, but it's very troubling because, again, we're talking about these choices families have to make, which is do they not send their kid to school?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How do they figure out this ride share?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Or what I have heard happened.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Parents take a risk on their kids and remove paras from the busing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They remove bus paras from the bus so that the kids could go to school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And to take away a service that a kid needs

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: so that they can simply go to school like every other kid in New York City is a pretty heartbreaking thing to hear and sort of egregious that parents are forced to make that choice because we can't provide paras for our kids.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So what steps are being taken to recruit and train and put more paras on the buses that these children can get to school?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Yeah, we completely agree that this is an area that we have to focus on.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And the approach that we're taking is to focus on the

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: we've been taking is to work with schools to ensure that first they're identifying kids that require the service in advance of the start of school

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: second that they're posting this is a procession activity that's just that's posted locally the principals are working with within the the base of school bus power professionals that are available to them within the school to identify somebody who can who can ride with the student

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: So that is the first and most critical step is building awareness and ensuring that our schools are arranging the services locally to the extent that they can.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: They're also working with...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm sorry to understand.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What is the recruitment effort?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, is it individual schools just posting it on their bulletin board?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: That's not how it should be, but it is a local posting.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: So a principal, a transportation coordinator would work across the school to identify a staff member who will be serving in that school bus paraprofessional role.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It just sounds like another area where...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You should be coordinating with some of the other departments, the Office of Students with Disabilities, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like the teaching and learning, like all of these departments, which I guess they don't have anymore, but all these other divisions within the DOE, it doesn't sound like what's been happening has been working.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It doesn't sound like putting it on the bulletin board

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: or maybe putting it in principles weekly is enough.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I'm asking what steps, other additional steps, besides what hasn't been working fully, is your office taking to recruit more paras?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So these 350 plus,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: kids can get on the bus and get to school.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: I completely understand.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And, you know, just trying to walk you through the process of how, you know, services are arranged locally at the school.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: We're also providing support from the district level to identify powers that can be deployed to support this work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What does that support look like?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: The district will contact neighboring schools that have and seek to support in the recruitment of paraprofessionals.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: We're also utilizing substitute paraprofessionals to the extent that they can become available.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And then if services cannot be identified through a UFT staff member, we're looking at contracted paraprofessional support.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: So we just this year have rolled out new related service contracts with new agencies, primary, secondary, tertiary agencies by district, and new agencies that are supporting specifically on paraprofessional services.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: So we're meeting with those new agencies regularly right now, looking at lists of students that need to be arranged, and we're working with them to get services in place.

chapters.summary: Brewer follows up on why penalties are not collected and how scorecards are used; DOE says it is reviewing enforcement and will publish more data.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer follows up on penalties and contractor scorecards

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And so we are hopeful with these new contracts as we support new agencies that this is going to help.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: But to your point, we need to be able to work with our DOE staff and get that happening a little bit more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The contracts are already implemented, so it is in the process of being done.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It is in the process.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is there a timeline, any sort of timeline?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: So the new agency started in September.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: So we're making new relationships.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: They're doing lots of outreach and staffing power professionals to come on board, and we're working with them to provide both support and accountability to ensure that everybody's moving with urgency to get all these services in place.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: And we're also working with families to leverage the interim measures that are in place through travel reimbursement, through ride share to ensure the kids are coming to school every day as that's happening.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How many parents have been recruited through these efforts since September?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: That's a number I can get back to you after the hearing, but it's something that I can certainly provide.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, is it more than zero?

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: It is more than zero, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: When I asked that question in one of the previous hearings, they couldn't tell me.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm glad you tell me it's more than zero, but you don't have an estimate as to how many.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: I can get you one.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, we'll be expecting that information.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Now, paras, nurses, these aren't the only workforce issues that we're facing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
