utterances.text: I mean, we have routes that are doubled up, and I think in the past year we had said there's a workforce shortage, or the companies have said there's not enough drivers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So if you could first walk us through what training a driver must complete before working on a New York City school bus, and if that's different for a stop to school or curb to school, generally for students with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yeah, so very much appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: In terms of the idea of recruiting drivers, we actually post all of our driver requirements.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: New York State Department of Motor Vehicles has all their information posted on what it takes to get a CDL, as well as New York State Education Department posts all their information on what needs to be a school bus driver.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We post that as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Certainly there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What do you mean post it?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It's on our info hub.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: It's on our website.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: You could actually see, you know, what are the requirements, the training requirements, what's the AED first aid, where's the glucogen training, what are the behind-the-wheel driving times.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: That's all posted information, so I could share that with you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: John, I don't know if you want to talk a little bit about the distinction between the training requirements on stop-to-school and curb-to-school, but certainly there is additional training for students with additional needs.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Yes, so in addition to the trainings that Deputy Chancellor Moran mentioned, we also have Vision Zero training, which applies to all school bus drivers across stop to school and curb to school.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Vision Zero training meaning how to safely operate a school bus in the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: There's always been standard trainings on how to safely drive a school bus that apply nationwide, but we all know driving in New York City is unique from driving anywhere else, especially a giant yellow vehicle.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: So this training was designed in conjunction with DCAS and DOT about

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: what it means to safely drive in New York, factoring in things like bike lanes and all just the unique circumstances that present themselves as you try to drive a vehicle through the city.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: So that's standard across both service populations.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: That's required annually.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: As it relates to supporting students on curb-to-school routes, students with disabilities, there's a training required annually as well.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: and how to responsibly support students with special needs on the bus as their disability may manifest themselves in certain ways in terms of like certain behaviors or things like that, making sure they're addressed and handled properly based on

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: best practices for supporting those students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I just want to clarify, you have some visible disabilities and some invisible disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Some are physical, some are not physical, and I just want to clarify that they are trained to

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: to recognize and respond to all sorts of different disability classifications.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: We also partner with John Hammer's team on certain strategies to enhance those trainings.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: We do supportive trainings as well.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: If we see an issue or a particular school or some routes where issues are manifesting themselves, we could do more targeted training to those drivers to support those exact individual students.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: So we're moving from just a broad-based training to actually addressing individual needs as well.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And then you post on the website, someone applies, how long does it take from hiring a new driver until that driver starts driving?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: I think it's six to eight is the last predictive that we were shared in terms of getting behind the wheel time in class.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Six to eight what?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Weeks.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Sorry.

chapters.summary: A foster care advocate testifies that students in foster care often lose bus service when they change placements and that coordination between agencies is poor.
chapters.title: Public witness describes bus service for students in foster care

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Could have been months.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Yeah, this background checks, fingerprinting.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Well, in New York City, it could be more than six to eight months.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So six to eight weeks, but they've been guaranteed a job.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And in that six to eight weeks, are they training or they're just waiting for some months?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: So a company has to nominate and bring them, you know, impose the position.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: So I don't want to say they're guaranteed, but I think the example would be with Nice Bus where I have them.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: deliberate relationship, yes, they would be guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: If they entered our driver safety program, successfully completed and completed the CDL requirements and all the OPI background checks, yes, they would be guaranteed a job.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So you've spoken about

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You've spoken about posting the jobs, both in terms of paraprofessionals and in terms of the drivers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We have a lot of students in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Are there any efforts, you know, for the students who, for whom college may not be their path,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: is there any outreach done within our schools or within CUNY to work with them for training programs to say, you know, being a bus driver is like a very good career path.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, you can work for New York City, you could take people, you know, kids where they need to go.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's really important.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: For our city and the pay, you know, this is the pay scale.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is your office making any efforts to coordinate with other divisions within the DOE or with, I don't know, Future Ready to recruit directly from our schools, from our high schools?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So for students age 21 and above, yes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: The CDL does have a requirement that is not your traditional motor vehicle for a teenager, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So for a CDL, you have to be 21.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So we've had some conversations at Mapperlin as well with our District 79 team about adults in our settings that we could share this opportunity with you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So I'll come back.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I don't know if I have stats at the ready.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: But it has been something we've been talking with our District 79 partners.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So discussing, but has any program been implemented to recruit students or to do any sort of outreach directly to the students?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Not a standalone program, more referral-based.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But what you're testifying to is that there is consideration to do that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yes, we'd like to continue to grow that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think it's important for kids to see this as a job-ready opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It looks like someone does have something.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Yeah, if I could jump in here, I think this is a tremendous opportunity for collaboration.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: I appreciate you lifting it up.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: It's a partnership that we have established with Future Ready through SYEP to have students trained to serve as District 75 paraprofessionals over the summer, and that's work that started this year.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to speak to the cohort of young adults who served as paraprofessionals this summer.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: So that's an example of ways that we're starting this work and would love to work with Deputy Chancellor Moran's team to consider ways that we can expand it to other roles that we need critically.

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: Just to close the loop on one piece, I'm still waiting for the full number on

utterances.speaker: John Hammer
utterances.text: contracted paraprofessional support, but I do know that the District 75 team was able to secure over 200 paraprofessionals to support with school bus transportation through our agencies this fall.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In 2024 to 2025, the Office of People Transportation investigated 340 cases involving bus

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: company employees, 178 of them alleging corporal punishment.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How many were substantiated and what happened to those employees?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: So I just want to make sure when cases are reported, we make sure we follow through and investigate it.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And so, John, I don't know if you brought each update as it relates to corporal punishment.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: I don't have updates on corporal punishment investigations.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: If we do get an allegation about that, it's immediately referred to an SCI investigation, which has a timeline associated with it.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: I don't have the stats on that, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: But we can get you a result of those investigations like a tracker and share that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The Comptroller found in the 2024-2025 school year,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: the DOE held no corrective action meetings and required no corrective action plans, even for companies with the highest complaint and delay rates.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How many companies are on a corrective action plan today?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: Today there is one company under a corrective action plan, and I would like to correct the record about that audit.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: We provided during the audit process evidence of companies during that time period that did go under corrective action plans.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: It was provided during the audit.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: I'm not sure why that report indicates it was zero.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: There was two.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And which company is under a corrective action plan?

chapters.summary: Joseph asks about timelines for implementing IEP transportation accommodations; DOE says it is working with schools but acknowledges delays.
chapters.title: Council Member Joseph follows up on IEP transportation timelines

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: We won't chair the company specifically.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I don't believe it's a matter of public record right now, so we're going to talk to our lawyers and come back to you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, talk to your lawyers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think this is, you know, the transparency that we're demanding in this council, whether through legislation or here, would require us to know what's going on with our bus companies that we send our children on.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: I think, in fairness, corrective action is an opportunity to correct poor performance, and we'd like to maintain that environment if we can, and if it's something that is a matter of public record, we'll certainly share it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How many corrective action meetings has the DOE held since the audit with this, I guess, one company?

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: There's been a series of them since the corrective action plan began.

utterances.speaker: John Benson
utterances.text: It's probably less than five or less.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: During the 2024, I know you were asked about some of the damages this year, but during the 24-25 school year, DUI could have assessed $44.3 million in damages for failing to log in the GPS tracking.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It only assessed $1.7 million.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Has the practice changed since then?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yes, that was during the pilot period.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: And now it's required.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's required.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And you mentioned, I think, $200-something thousand.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is that for a particular company or that was for?

utterances.speaker: Kevin Moran
utterances.text: Broadly, September, October for all vendors.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: For all vendors, okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I do just want to, just going back to the workforce development element, you cited Future Ready, I believe, or we both spoke about Future Ready.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think this is another opportunity for the Office of People Transportation to do some advocacy and lobbying.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Because this is another program that constantly feels like it's under threat.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We constantly have to feel like we have to fight and justify funding things like Future Ready.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it gives students incredible opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It gives the city incredible leeway in solving a lot of its biggest problems, like transportation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so I'm just going to assume we have your commitment to lobby for this program or for expansion of the Future Ready program.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Look forward to working with you on this.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We'll be sending follow-up questions to the Department of Education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think there were a number of unresolved questions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We'll get those, and we'll be sending some follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If you could just give me one more moment.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I just want to ask one more time.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There was specific data about routing information that we requested, and I will say on the record, the data that we received was incomplete.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so we are once again now publicly requesting that data.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And then...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I have a number of questions again on late reports, which I won't read them now, but we will be requesting them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There's a lot of information we deserve as it relates to school transportation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There's a lot of work to do here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There's a lot of work to do around transparency.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There's a lot of work to do on the routing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Which appears to be the number one issue for a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Unfortunately, without the data, we were unable to exemplify that point.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There's questions, like I said, of workforce development about the contracts that the DOE is entering and what we're actually getting for it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And at the end of the day, this is all in service to our students, and the students who need the very most support.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Every single time we hear about a parent who can't send their kid to school, who's waiting out for the bus to come, for a kid who's on the bus for two hours, it is heartbreaking and much less than what any child in this city deserves.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I look forward to continuing our work together to make sure every child has transit to school, that it's dignified.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and safe for all of our children.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I want to thank the DOE for coming into that and the mayor's office for coming as well.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We will call our first panel in a moment.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I will now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

chapters.summary: A pre-K parent testifies that their child's bus arrives at inconsistent times and that young children are left waiting in cold weather.
chapters.title: Public witness describes bus service for pre-K students

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance slip with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's oversight topic.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Within 72 hours of the hearing, audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: For our first panel, I'd like to call Nico, or formerly Nicholas Hernandez, and Lupe Hernandez.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we're only allowed to clap for students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Otherwise, none of that in here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Nico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: I'm an eighth grader at School of the Future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Since going to School of the Future, I started riding the school bus again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: I spent all of last year waiting an hour every day after dismissal for the bus to drop me off at home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: We had early dismissal on Fridays, but the bus still came at the normal pickup time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: I just wanted to get home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: During the summer months, I still go to school and had the most trouble during ESY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: This past summer, we had some really hot days, and one of them, I got really sick on my ride home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: The bus had AC, but it was not enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: I had a bad headache, and I felt like I was going to throw up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: I would like to participate in travel training, but there is not enough funding to provide for students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Travel training is very hard to access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Even my mom, who is a parent leader, can't find information for travel training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: I understand there are students that need it more than me, but every student that's ready should get an opportunity to become more independent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: This year, I'm ready to transition into using public transportation, but I am unable to because of the Chancellor's regulations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: It says if a student takes a school bus, they cannot have an OmniCard for public transportation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: This isn't fair for the student.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: who take the school bus and have extracurricular activities or want to attend after school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: When Mayor Adams announced Omni in 2024, he says, when you are a student, you could use your Omni card to pick up your siblings, go to an appointment somewhere, or go to the library in your community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: If I ever wanted to go to a library outside of my community, I am unable to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Because I don't have an OmniCard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: My brother has never been to the big public library by Central Park because he walks to school, so he didn't get an OmniCard either.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: He still deserves an OmniCard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Traveling in New York City is expensive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: As a student athlete, I can't go to my games on the weekends, which was promised when Omni was announced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Just because I ride a school bus doesn't mean I don't play sports or have games on the weekends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: I, too, would benefit from having an OmniCard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: The DOE can change the Chancellor's regulations to have Omni for all students, but they say we need more money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: So I'm here asking City Council to please fund on-time buses, travel training for all, and an OmniCard for all New York City students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Nico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: Thank you, the chair and the education committee for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: My name is Lupe Hernandez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: She, her, a pronouns, and I am a New York City public school parent, proud to have my son here advocating and voicing all of his concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: And I have spent a majority of his life since he was two years old that he's on a bus advocating for not only on-time busing, but more efficient routing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: I kind of want to talk about some of the things that I heard today from the DOE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: I want to just stress the fact that I appreciate the council for passing many of the busing packages, including Local Laws 32 that we spoke about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: And I'm not surprised that the DOE...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: Handed over the half data that they were supposed to publish on October 31st.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: Just want to flag that they've never been in compliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: This data has never been published on time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: And that is a problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: Makes it hard for that transparency bill to actually be effective.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: The VIA app, as a parent that tries to use this application every day and has seen my driver's phone online but says offline for me,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: is a very different experience than what I heard today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: Majority of the parents that I know, yes, you may be able to get it to work, but you can sometimes see your bus in a different country, which we know is not happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: We also don't know where my child is.

chapters.summary: Lee asks about the VIA contract and missed deadlines; DOE says it is phasing out old routing software and working with VIA to meet requirements.
chapters.title: Council Member Lee follows up on VIA contract and missed deadlines

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: It knows where the driver of that particular bus is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: Should a child, which has happened, get on the wrong school bus, you're tracking the bus that your child should be on, but not necessarily your child.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: The ridership pilot that my son is actually participating in this year only shows me when he boards the bus if I'm on the app at the time that the bus is in front of my house.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: But as you mentioned earlier, we don't have access to seeing any of the history beyond in real time.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm a little harsher on adults than I am on students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I do want to clarify something, if it wasn't clear, like for the record, that the DOE was late on the reports per the local law.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I don't think we've gone through them to know if they're complete or incomplete.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We had requested separate data from them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I know we're talking.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I know we're going to get the information from them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But I just wanted to, in all fairness to them, clarify that they were not.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: To my knowledge, incomplete with the things demanded of local law, the local laws.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Nico, can I just ask you, you're a city kid?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You like New York City?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What are some of your favorite places to go in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: I like to go to the, it's, I think it's called the Museum of Natural History.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Oh my God, yeah, of course.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do you go to the Hall of Biodiversity?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: No, I haven't been there.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Oh, you've got to get to that one.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And did you weigh yourself on Jupiter?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's when you walk and you go all the way downstairs.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You got that ecosystem and that giant glass ball.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You got to go back.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's where you have to go back.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Anywhere else you'd like to go in the city?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: I've been, I think it is called...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: It was a museum about the Civil War, but I forgot what it was called.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Maybe it's the Civil War Museum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I don't know if that's the name of the museum.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I just feel like that would be a good title for it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, you just named two really, we have like really great places here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's a place unlike any other, but per your testimony, you don't have...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Access to an OmniCard, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And what does that mean for you that you don't have an OmniCard even though you live in a city that has a Museum of Natural History and the Civil War Museum, whatever it's called?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Well, it like means that I can't go to like places where I can like learn like about, you know, about history, about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: science about like

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Many things.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: And not having an OmniCard just limits my, like, learning.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, and I got to tell you, it limits your learning and your experience.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I got to tell you, we should be doing nothing in this city that limits your learning.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Nico, you did great.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to thank you for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This is a very good experience for you to come and advocate for yourself and for students all over the city.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They're all, whether they know it or not, they're all grateful to you, and you're making an impact on their lives.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So thank you for coming to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Our next panel is Donovan Swanson.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Randy Levine.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Laurie Podvisir, Lauren Newman, and Naya Berg.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we can start on my left, your right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yes, and you can begin.

chapters.summary: A shelter resident testifies that bus service is frequently canceled and that families are not notified, causing children to miss school.
chapters.title: Public witness describes bus service for students in shelters

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: State your name for the record and begin your two-minute testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Make sure your mic's on, the red light should be on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Councilman Burdenowitz.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: My name is Laura Newman, and I'm the Associate Director of Advocacy at Transportation Alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: I have the immense honor of mentoring dozens of New York City students through our Youth Activist Committee, where young people come together to fight for transportation justice for students and by students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: For nearly two years, our students have been fighting for expanding student omni after recognizing a glaring inequality in our current system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: Students who rely on yellow school buses like Nico are excluded from the same transit benefits available to their peers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: Despite often

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: facing some of the greatest transportation challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: With tens of thousands of school bus delays each year, our students know firsthand that unreliable transportation creates real barriers to education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: They recognize that Student Omni is not a replacement for school buses, but it can give students another reliable way to get to school while building the confidence and independence to navigate their city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: The city must fix its school bus system, and we urge you to take seriously the solutions proposed by the advocates in the Better Buses Coalition to ensure no student is left behind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: But we also need to think beyond the immediate crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: Investing in travel training as a complementary strategy would give more students the skills and confidence to use public transit, offer families greater flexibility, and help ease pressure on overcrowded bus routes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: Additionally, Chancellor's Regulation 801 has not been updated since 2000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: This outdated regulation governs student transportation and currently locks the 150,000 students who are bused out of receiving student Omni cards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: This in turn places this burden on their families to cover.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Newman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I think you heard from the DOE that there seemed to be an openness to amending that Chancellor's regulations.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They didn't cite it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I didn't cite it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But we did discuss.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Omni cards for the students who take busing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So you can be sure that we're going to be following up with that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Genowitz.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: I'm in the Education Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: I'm here on behalf of the Brooklyn Borough President, Antonio Reynoso.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: My name is Donovan Swanson, Director of Programs and Education Engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: Due to time, I'm going to try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: You have our full testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: Just want to acknowledge that the Borough President is supporting both the intro as well as the resolution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: He's in lockstep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: He's also a parent of a child who receives and is entitled to services and has actually opted out of it given his previous experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: You know, we could say a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: We just want to acknowledge that as a system, we're also struggling with enrollment, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: And even in the Comptroller's most recent report, decline of 3% just within the year, it's still also noted that the ones we're serving are those in the highest economic need, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: Including our students with disabilities, those entitled IEPs, as well as our students in temporary housing, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: All on the rise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: And so we really do need to fix the system, and it's an urgent need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: You know, we could look at just looking at some of the data that was publicly available to date from 2025,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: roughly 22% of cases or that roughly associated to 7,000 plus cases of delays that weren't associated to things outside of the driver's control, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: So we excluded weather, traffic, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: 22% of cases still unexplained, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: That is in a system that's not accounting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: holding the standard of quality that our families deserve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: I want to acknowledge that it was also brought up, the number of hours that students are traveling in that same

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: data set, 58,000 students experienced bus rides lasting one to two hours with approximately 1,000 students enduring rides of two hours or more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: Still unacceptable, especially when you factor in the Councilmember Juan's previous question around with even across boroughs, which we know our students in temporary housing, given McKinney-Vento, are entitled to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: So there's a number of things that we could talk about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: You know, we are definitely in support of the state legislation for EPP provisions because we need a new contract, and our PEP appointee is prepared to vote no, again, on a contract extension that does not get us to where we need to be as a city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Donovan Swanson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You raised a number of things, including students in temporary housing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I do want to point out, and I will point this out every time, that although there's a declining enrollment, we're doing everything we can, and the DOE, however hard they work,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If we continue to have a housing policy that only builds studio and one-bedroom apartments and maybe some two-bedroom apartments, we're going to continue to see an exodus of families from our city.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're going to continue to see families enter our shelter system, the families who, by the way, with children.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about driver wages and benefits; DOE says contract extensions include workforce protections and that state legislation would help.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse follows up on bus driver wages and benefits

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Who make up the vast majority of shelter residents.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so our housing policy really is an education policy.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And until we change our housing policy to build more two-bedrooms and any three-bedroom apartments, we're going to continue to see families leaving our system.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're going to continue to see families ending up in temporary housing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Randy?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: My name is Randy Levine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: I'm Policy Director at Advocates for Children of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: Every year we hear from hundreds of families experiencing significant challenges with school bus service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: The challenges disproportionately impact students with disabilities and students who are homeless or in foster care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: We were particularly concerned at the start of this school year when thousands of students with disabilities did not have bus vendors for their routes, and the calls have not stopped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: In the first two weeks of November alone, we have heard from the families of a student with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: leading all year for bus service to their District 75 school because no vendor has selected the route.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: A student living in shelter waiting all year for bus service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: A student whose bus failed to show up and then lost its bus driver and then arrived 20 minutes late and then an hour early and ultimately dropped the student from the route.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: A first grader.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: Who is on the bus from 6.45 to 10 a.m., even though the school and home are in the same borough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: A student whose IEP requires limited travel time, whose bus arrives home an hour and a half late from a school less than two miles from home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: Students living in shelter who were displaced by a fire,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: whose busing took weeks to reroute and are now experiencing late arrivals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: A medically fragile student who has been out of school for the past month due to serious safety concerns involving the bus vendor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: When the parent raised these concerns, bus staff became irate and cursed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: A 12th grader with a disability who regularly arrives at school late.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: Students whose IEP mandated busing was improperly discontinued last week with no notice to families and many more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: This is just in November.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: The city must act, including by taking a number of steps now, which we've laid out in our written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: In addition, the city must rebid its decades-old contracts, which date back to 1979 and are not meeting the needs of today's students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: One year ago, the PEP rejected the five-year extension of these contracts, extending the contracts only through June 2028.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: The city must use this opportunity to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: make major improvements to school bus service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: That's why we support Resolution 735.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: We also support Intro 835.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair and the committee, for having this today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: My name is Naya Berg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Director of New York Appleseed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: We convene the Road to Better Busing Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: There's a lot in my testimony, so I'm going to keep it short.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: The system needs to be rebuilt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: It is the current expectation that New York City Yellow Bus Service can reliably, safely, and efficiently carry nearly 150,000 students

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: every day, roughly 60,000 of them students with disabilities, all while using ineffective stopgap measures, unreliable routing software, and outdated school bus contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: The school bus contracts have largely not been updated since 1979.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: We are giving this system, I think, the classic New York apartment paint job, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: It's a fresh coat of paint over every single crack, and we continue to pretend these cracks aren't there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: Rather than rebid on these bus contracts, we have spent more than four decades extending and patching them with amendments, and these patches just don't fix the foundation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: Last November, as many of my folks on this table have said, the city tried to push through five-year extensions, and advocates and folks came together to say that that was egregious.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: agreed to a three-year deal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: The panel for education policy voted down these long-term extensions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: City and New York City public schools have told the PEP that they needed these three years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: We are one year later, two years remaining before it expires in June 2028.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: And PEP members have already said in October they passed a resolution saying that they would not approve another extension.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: We need to figure out what the plan is next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: And the same fragility that we have with these contracts show up in problems the city could tackle right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: We had a discussion about VIA and the promise of efficient routing that hasn't come to pass in the last seven years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: And we have more and more parents that are relying on AirTags than they actually are relying on the app that supposedly does work, even though we are getting an influx of folks that say it does not for them.

chapters.summary: A parent of a child with autism testifies that the bus environment is overwhelming and that drivers are not trained to support sensory needs.
chapters.title: Public witness describes bus service for students with autism

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: There's many more things that we've talked about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: I will just say that we need to do better, and New York City must operate with urgency on these issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nyah Berg
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Hi, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I want to thank you guys for holding this hearing, and especially you, Chair Denowitz, for your pressing questions with the DOE in terms of transparency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And to your really smart supporting staff on both sides.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Smartest people.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Smartest people right next to me.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the team, and I just have to say, you can pause the time because I do have to say this.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There's an incredible team that you don't see up here, not just my staff, the council staff, the finance division, the data team was working like all night on some of the stuff, and of course the education staff.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: that you don't all get to see.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I thanked them in the beginning, but they really do an incredible amount of work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I see some of them here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Oh, there they are.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You should wave to them and thank them on the way out if you don't, because a lot of the questions and a lot of the data and all that, it's really due to them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I just want to take that moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: These two and the ones you don't see.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We all appreciate all of you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I lead the policy work at Include NYC, and I don't want to echo all that has been said, but what I do want to stress is the implications of, you know, an inferior system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And what that looks like for parents, and you guys hit upon that at multiple times, but the stress, the additional stress that parents face of kids with disabilities is unreal in terms of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: tasks and things that need to be done and the amount of time and steps it takes to just do one thing, especially in a bureaucratic, bogged-down system such as this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: The other point I want to make that I feel needs to be lifted

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: as much as possible is when kids get pulled out of school early at the end of the day or they arrive late, it also means that they are being excluded from their school communities and their classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And this is a civil rights issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And, you know, we don't often think of framing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Or we don't, the public doesn't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: perceive these issues to the extent that we see them, you know, from a bird's eye view collectively and, you know, cumulatively what this means for a student every year in terms of the amount of time

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: that they're excluded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And so we press on you all to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: get data from the DOE that focuses on the extent in which kids with disabilities spend time with general ed students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Because in the morning and afternoon during busing time, it is also opportunity for kids to gain soft skills, which will lead to better outcomes later on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So I'll just leave it at that, and you can read our full testimony recommendations here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'd like to thank this panel.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: For their testimony and I know a lot of you were at the roundtable we held beforehand and for all the work you do

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: outside of the here, not just your testimony, but you do a lot of work helping students with disabilities in various ways, advocating for fair and safe busing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I want to thank you for all the work you do outside of this room as well.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Our next panel is Elizabeth Caron, Francesca Mercedes, Hannah Mercuris, Suhali Mendez, and Erica King.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we did hear that, you know, just to follow up on what Lori said, we did hear that phrase, least restrictive environment, this idea that we want our students in the setting that makes sense for them, not restricted by a bus schedule in this case.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They should be able to experience everything that school has to offer.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A phrase you shouldn't have to say out loud, but we do say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're going to mix things up.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We'll go crazy.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We'll start on my right and your left.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You'll go first.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, press the red button so it turns red.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Because I can't hear me.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Genowitz and members of the Committee of the Education.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks about incident reporting and safety protocols; DOE describes a new incident response team but acknowledges reporting gaps.
chapters.title: Council Member Schulman follows up on bus safety and incident reporting

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: My name is Francesca Mercedes, and I'm an education specialist at Children's Aid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify on school transportation for students in foster care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: For more than 170 years, Children's Aid has helped young people reach their full potential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Today, we work alongside more than 900 children and youth involved in foster care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: When a child enters foster care or changes placements,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Remaining in their school can provide critical stability, yet students can wait weeks or even months for an assigned bus route.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: I currently work with a seven-year-old child in foster care who attends a D75 school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: He has cerebral palsy, a seizure disorder, and uses a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: And he has mandated transportation on his IEP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Over the summer, he moved homes, and since the first day of school, he has been waiting for a route.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: He's still waiting today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Because his foster parent cannot transport him every day, Children's Aid staff has stepped in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Since September, at least eight staff, including myself, from case planners to supervisors, have taken turns taking him to and from school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: I'm the one who creates the weekly schedules, and some staff have to wake up at 5 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: We do this because he deserves to be in school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: But I keep asking myself, if a child in foster care with significant disabilities and transportation mandated on his IEP cannot get a bus route, then who can?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: The DOE informed us that there is no route available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: So where does that leave us?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: We need the city to provide safe, reliable transportation from the moment a child enters foster care until permanent bus route is in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: No child should miss school or lose a source of stability because of transportation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: It cannot be arranged quickly enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Francesca Mercedes
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: Hey, thank you so much for the opportunity to speak today about school bus service in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: My name is Erica King.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: I work at Advocates for Children of New York, and I'm testifying on behalf of the Transition Alliance, which is a coalition of more than 20 organizations dedicated to improving transition planning for students with disabilities in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: I'm here today to urge the city to expand travel training, which teaches students with disabilities to navigate public transit independently and reduce reliance on yellow bus service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: School bus service has been unreliable for years, and students with disabilities bear a disproportionate share of the harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: Many have IEPs that mandate yellow bus service because they cannot navigate public transit alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: I recently worked with such a student, and his family moved over the summer, and much like others that we heard today, they couldn't figure out who to call to get their address updated, and it took New York CPS four weeks to assign a new route and driver,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: and the bus didn't actually reach his door until October 22nd, so he missed the first six weeks of 10th grade, and his pickup time was at 5.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: Travel training offers is an option that does not depend on bus vendors, drivers, or route assignments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: Through one-on-one instruction, students learn to navigate public transit, build confidence, and agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: The D75 program serves only a fraction of the students who need it, and wait lists keep hundreds out each year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: We call on the city to expand travel training in D1 through 32 schools, increase capacity in D75, and contract with experienced community-based organizations to train students directly and build the capacity of school staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: Each student who travels in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: independently, freeze a seat on a strained bus system, lowering city transportation costs, and gains a reliable way to reach schools, the Natural History Museum, therapies, internships, and eventually, hopefully, employment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica King
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the opportunity to speak today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nico Hernandez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Dynowitz and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: My name is Suhali Mendez and I'm the Policy and Legislative Coordinator at New York Lawyers for the Public Interest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: And I want to thank you for holding this hearing on school transportation services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: Today I urge the Council to strengthen transparency and accountability in the school transportation system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: Along with improving service for students with disabilities and continuing to advance the transition to electric school buses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: School transportation is more than a logistical issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: It is an educational access, disability rights, as well as a public health issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: First, New York Lawyers for the Public Interest supports Intro 835, which will require the Department of Education to publicly report on school bus delays as well as route performances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: Families deserve clear, accessible information on how the system is functioning, and policymakers need data to identify and address persistent problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: Second, the city must improve service reliability for students with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: When buses are late, fail to arrive, or cannot meet,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: students needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: Students lose instructional time and families are forced to make alternative arrangements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: Reliable transportation is essential in ensuring students can fully participate in their education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: Finally, we urge the city to stay on track toward a fully electric school bus fleet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: Electric school buses can reduce harmful air pollution, improve children's health, and deliver the greatest benefits

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: to environmental justice communities that have long burned a disproportionate burden of transportation-related pollution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: We urge the Council to advance Intro 835, strengthen oversight of student transportation services, and ensure continued progress towards an equitable electric school bus transition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suhali Mendez
utterances.text: Thank you for allowing me the opportunity to testify.

chapters.summary: A Queens parent testifies that bus routes are often combined, leading to long rides and late arrivals, and calls for more direct routes.
chapters.title: Public witness describes bus service for students in Queens

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think you all rehearsed getting it under two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think this is great.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This is fantastic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lupe Hernandez
utterances.text: No promises.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: My name is Hannah Mercurius and I'm a senior attorney at Brooklyn Defender Services in the education unit of our civil justice practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: BDS is a public defense office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: We represent approximately 40,000 people each year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: in Brooklyn and Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Thank you to the Committee on Education and Chair Dunwitz for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: City Council has heard directly from families who have experienced busing delays about how harmful those delays are to students, especially students with disabilities and students experiencing housing instability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: BDS is focusing our testimony on the impact of those delays for families and students experiencing surveillance by the Administration for Children's Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: ACS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: The ripple effect of the city's failure to get students to school is not felt just by students, but by their siblings and families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Busing delays increase the possibility that ACS will seek to separate families, as scrutiny of school attendance is part of every ACS inquiry or monitoring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Because strong school attendance is so often conflated with child safety, every day that a child misses school increases the likelihood that education professionals or shelter staff will call the SCR, the Statewide Central Register of Child Abuse and Maltreatment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: While ACS and the DOE have issued joint guidance clarifying that school absences aren't an adequate reason to call the SCR, these calls persist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: This fall, our office has worked with many families who have either court-ordered ACS supervision or new investigations where busing delays and school absences heightened ACS's concerns about child safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Parents who are experiencing ACS investigations or surveillance are under immense scrutiny and stress every time a bus route is delayed or the bus is late, and any time the bus is late, their stress and fear is heightened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: In addition to the harm to children's education and their learning, school bus delays also prevent parents and caregivers from getting to other services that are essential to their family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Medical appointments for young children, mental health services, substance use disorder treatment, domestic violence support services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Parents spend hours transporting their children to school and wait outside the school building until dismissal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah Mercurius
utterances.text: We'll submit written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Dinowitz, to the staff members and the Education Committee for the opportunity to testify here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
utterances.text: My name is Elizabeth Curran, and I am a senior supervising attorney in the New York Legal Assistance Group in our special education unit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
utterances.text: As many other advocates have shared, transportation problems are one of the top issues that we deal with, and year after year, we see that they are only getting worse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
utterances.text: DOE's failure to implement IEP-mandated transportation services is widespread, and I'd like to lift up some examples of how this is impacting our clients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
utterances.text: And another thing I'd like to highlight is many of these students are absent from school for long periods of time and there is no makeup instruction that is being provided to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
utterances.text: The only way families can really access that is pursuing a due process complaint, which is not an easy thing to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
utterances.text: So just to share some examples, we have one student who missed 10 months of school from January of this year through October because he was never given a para.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
utterances.text: The para he was finally given quit after a few days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
utterances.text: He's still out of school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
utterances.text: Another client did not receive a bus route to his school for the entire summer, and his parents spent hours each day bringing him to and from school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Curran
